question: A 68 yr. old man came with pain and swelling of right knee. Ahlback grade 2 osteoarthritic changes were found on investigation. What is the further management?
exp: Ans. is 'd' i.e. Conservative Initial management of most of the patients of knee OA is conservative or non-operative.Campbell operative orthopaedics writes - "Osteoarthritis of the knee can cause symptoms ranging from mild to disabling. Initial management of most patients should be nonoperative".Surgical management is needed when the conservative management fails.Surgical management in brief:The choice of surgical procedure depends on the patient's age and activity demand, severity of the disease and the number of knee compartments involved.Arthroscopic washout or debridement:It consists of trimming of degenerate meniscal tissue and osteophytesIt may delay the need for a more definitive procedure, especially in younger, active patients with localised degenerative arthritis that causes pain at rest without malalignment or instabilityIt may also be considered in active, older adults with mild to moderate OA Realignment osteotomy:High or proximal tibial osteotomy (HTO)-High tibial osteotomy is a procedure for the treatment of unicompartmental osteoarthritis of the knee (medial or lateral compartment osteoarthritis; usually it is medial; lateral compartment osteoarthritis is uncommon).Medial osteoarthritis is associated with varus deformity of the knee. Varus deformity causes stresses to be concentrated medially, accelerating degenerative changes in the medial part of the joint (similarly if the deformity is of valgus position, changes are accelerated in the lateral part).The biomechanical rationale for proximal tibial osteotomy in patients with unicompartmental osteoarthritis of the knee is "unloading" of the involved joint compartment by correcting the malalignment and redistributing the stresses on the knee joint.Thus medial osteoarthritis is treated by a varus correcting osteotomy (k/a valgus osteotomy) and the uncommon lateral osteoarthritis corrected by valgus correcting osteotomy (k/a varus osteotomy).According to Ebnezar (3/e p547) High tibial osteotomy is done for varus deformity less than 15deg and valgus deformity less than 12deg.Supracondylar or distal femoral osteotomy- - distal femoral osteotomy is done for correction of valgus deformity more than 12 to 15deg (Ref: Campbell's Orthopaedics 11/e chapter 25)Total knee arthroplasty:It is done for older patients with advanced OA that causes incapacitating pain and disability or young patients with tricompartmental (medial and lateral tibio femoral and patellofemoral) disease. But it should be delayed in young patients as long as possible as prostheses may wear out over time and may need further revision surgery.Unicompartmental arthroplasty:In carefully selected patients with either medial or lateral osteoarthritis, it is becoming a viable alternative to TKA and HTO.Knee arthrodesis:Arthrodesis is indicated less commonly than arthroplasty. However arthrodesis results in a stiff knee which is a severe disability.Ahlback's grading of osteoarthritisAhlback's grading is radiological grading of osteoarthritis. question: For international comparisons, perinatal moality rate is calculated as late fetal deaths (28 weeks gestation or more) plus early neonatal deaths (first week) in a year per: September 2011
exp: Ans. B: 1,000 live bihs For international comparisons, the WHO committee on the prevention of Perinatal Moality and Morbidity recommend a more precise formulation: "Late foetal and early neonatal deaths weighing over 1000 gram at bih, expressed as a ratio per 1000 live bihs weighing over 1000 gram at bih" Perinatal moality (PNM)/ Perinatal death It refers to the death of a fetus or neonate and is the basis to calculate the perinatal moality rate. Variations in the precise definition of the perinatal moality exist specifically concerning the issue of inclusion or exclusion of early fetal and late neonatal fatalities. The World Health Organization defines perinatal moality as the "number of stillbihs and deaths in the first week of life per 1,000 live bihs", but other definitions have been used Fetal moality refers to stillbihs or fetal death. It encompasses any death of a fetus after 20 weeks of gestation or 500 gm. In some definitions of the PNM early fetal moality (week 20-27 gestation) is not included, and the PNM may only include late fetal death and neonatal death. Fetal death can also be divided into death prior to labor, antenatal (antepaum) death, and death during labor, intranatal (intrapaum) death Early neonatal moality refers to a death of a live-born baby within the first seven days of life, while late neonatal moality covers the time after 7 days until before 28 days. The sum of these two represents the neonatal moality. Some definitions of the PNM include only the early neonatal moality. Neonatal moality is affected by the quality of in-hospital care for the neonate. Neonatal moality and postneonatal moality (covering the remaining 11 months of the first year of life) are reflected in the Infant Moality Rate. The PNMR refers to the number of perinatal deaths per 1,000 total bihs. It is usually repoed on an annual basis. It is a major marker to assess the quality of health care delivery.

This condition is sometimes seen in individuals with Trisomy 21, also known as Down syndrome. The most common cause of duodenal atresia is meiotic non-disjunction, a genetic error that occurs during the formation of gametes.

For example, hyperophic pyloric stenosis may manifest as a "Single Bubble" on an X-ray, while jejunum atresia can produce a "Triple Bubble" appearance. Tuberous Sclerosis is a genetic disorder characterized by mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 gene. The condition affects various organs in the body, including the central nervous system (CNS), kidneys, eyes, lungs, and heart.

In the CNS, tuberous sclerosis is often associated with epilepsy, which is the most common manifestation of the condition. The kidneys are also affected, with the most common tumor being a benign renal neoplasm called an angiomyolipoma. This type of tumor originates from perivascular epithelioid cells (PEComa) and consists of a mixture of vessels, smooth muscle, and fat in varying proportions.

In addition to these manifestations, tuberous sclerosis can also affect the eyes, where retinal glial hamartomas may occur. The lungs may be affected by pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis, a condition characterized by the growth of abnormal smooth muscle cells in the airways. The heart can also be affected, with the presence of rhabdomyomas.

On the skin, tuberous sclerosis is characterized by the presence of various hamartomas, including ash leaf patches, shagreen patches, and subungual fibromas. These lesions are benign and do not pose a significant health risk.

Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in Caucasian adults. It is caused by antibodies, usually autoantibodies, directed at antigens expressed on the surface of podocytes, including the M-type phospholipase A2 receptor 1. While most cases are idiopathic, a significant proportion are associated with other causes, such as heavy metal poisoning, drugs, infections, lupus, and tumors.

Approximately one-third of patients with idiopathic membranous nephropathy experience spontaneous remission, one-third remain in a nephrotic state, and one-third develop progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD). High doses of glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide may improve both the nephrotic syndrome and the long-term prognosis. However, due to the toxicity of these regimens, many nephrologists reserve such treatment for those with severe nephrotic syndrome or deteriorating renal function. Treatment of secondary membranous nephropathy is directed at the underlying cause.

question: The most reliable fetal parameter for estimation of gestational age in first trimester is:
exp: Ans. C. CRLGestational age (GA) in the first trimester is usually calculated from the fetal crown-rump length (CRL). This is the longest demonstrable length of the embryo or fetus, excluding the limbs and the yolk sac. The correlation between CRL and GA is excellent until approximately 12 weeks. No sex or race differences are appreciable, but maternal characteristics, such as age and smoking, may have a significant effect beyond 10-week gestation. The GA estimate has a 95% confidence interval of plus or minus 6 days, and it is most accurate between 7 and 10 weeks of pregnancy. Transabdominal ultrasonography may underestimate gestational age by an average of 1.6 days compared with transvaginal ultrasonography.

question: True regarding prothrombin time measurement?
exp:
Major screening tests of coagulation 

In all of these tests, blood is collected with a calcium-chelating anticoagulant (usually citrate) and then centrifuged to remove the erythrocytes, leukocyte and platelets.
The remaining platelet-poor plasma (PPP) serves as the substrate for these tests.
Depending upon the test, the phospholipid is added to the PPP to substitute for platelets and an activating agent is added.
The PPP is then recalcified and the time needed for a clot to form is measured.
The sample to be kept at room temperature if it is to be used for prothrombin time, Lupus anticoagulant or factor VII assays and to be kept at 4° C for other assays.
Once blood is drawn for testing, the tests should be completed within a time frame of 30 minutes to 2 hours. 

Measurement of prothrombin time

The PT measures the function of the extrinsic and common coagulation pathway. It is commonly used to monitor oral anticoagulant therapy.
Method:- A source of phospholipid and tissue thromboplastin (rabbit or human brain extract) is added to platelet poor plasma, and Ca2+ is added to initiate coagulation. The time for the appearance of fibrin strands (PT) is measured and is compared with the control.
Normal PT is 11- 13 seconds.

Measurement of Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT or aPTT)

The PTT and APTT are used to measure the function of intrinsic and common coagulation pathway. PTT and APTT are used to monitor heparin therapy.
PTT method:- Phospholipid is added to platelet poor plasma taken from blood that is anticoagulated with citrate. Clotting is then initiated by the addition of Ca2+. The time to the formation of first fibrin strands is PTT.
APTT method:- The APTT is performed in the same manner as PTT except for the addition of an activating agent such as kaolin or ellagic acid before recalcification.
Normal PTT is 28-35 seconds. 
Measurement of thrombin time
It tests the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, i.e., it screens thrombin-fibrinogen reaction.
Method:- Thrombin is added to the patient's platelet poor plasma and the time to fibrin strand formation is measured
Normal TT is 15- 20 seconds.
Other screening tests
These are:-

Platelet function tests ( bleeding time)
Screening for factor XIII
Other individual factor assay

2,3-DPG is synthesized within red blood cells (RBCs) from 3-phosphoglycerate, a product of glycolysis in the Embden-Meyerhof pathway. This highly charged anion binds to the P-chains of deoxyhemoglobin. One mole of deoxyhemoglobin binds one mole of 2,3-DPG.

In an equilibrium reaction, the binding of 2,3-DPG to deoxyhemoglobin shifts the reaction to the right, releasing oxygen. The reaction is:

HbO2 + 2,3-DPG = Hb - 2,3-DPG + O2

The concentration of 2,3-DPG and its affinity for hemoglobin can be affected by various factors, including:

* Increasing 2,3-DPG levels, such as in chronic hypoxia, high altitude, cyanotic congenital heart disease, anemia, acidosis, exercise, and certain hormonal changes (thyroid hormone, growth hormone, androgens, and pregnancy).
* Decreasing 2,3-DPG levels, such as in the presence of inosine, dihydroxyacetone, pyruvate, phosphate, stored blood, and fetal hemoglobin.
* Changes in pH, such as in alkalosis.

question: Malocclusion	representing	a transverse deficiency is often referred to as:
exp:
ACKERMAN-PROFITT SYSTEM OF CLASSIFICATION
CHARACTERISTIC 1 – ALIGNMENT
Intra arch alignment and symmetry are assessed as when seen in the occlusal view.
A dental arch is classified as ideal / crowded / spaced.
CHARACTERISTIC 2 – PROFILE
The profile can be convex / straight / concave.
This also includes the assessment of facial divergence, i.e. anterior or posterior divergence.
CHARACTERISTIC 3 – TRANSVERSE RELATIONSHIPS
They include transverse skeletal and dental relationships.
Buccal and palatal crossbites are noted. These are further subclassified as unilateral or bilateral.
Distinction is made between skeletal and dental crossbites.
CHARACTERISTIC 4 – CLASS
Here, the sagittal relationship of the teeth is assessed using the Angle classification as Class I / Class II / Class III.
A distinction is made between skeletal and dental malocclusions.
CHARACTERISTIC 5 – OVERBITE
Malocclusions are assessed in the vertical plane.

The primary function of MHC molecules is to display peptide fragments of protein antigens to antigen-specific T cells, allowing for recognition and activation of the immune response. MHC molecules are fundamental to the recognition of antigens by T cells and are linked to many autoimmune diseases. In humans, MHC molecules are referred to as human leukocyte antigens (HLA).

Based on their structure, cellular distribution, and function, MHC gene products are classified into two major classes. Class I MHC molecules are expressed on all nucleated cells and platelets. They are heterodimers consisting of a polymorphic alpha, or heavy, chain linked non-covalently to a smaller non-polymorphic protein called beta 2-microglobulin. Class I MHC molecules display peptides derived from proteins, such as viral and tumor antigens, that are located in the cytoplasm and usually produced in the cell. These peptides are recognized by CD8+ T lymphocytes, which are said to be class I MHC-restricted because they recognize peptides only when presented as a complex with class I MHC molecules.

Class II MHC molecules, encoded in the HLA-D region, are heterodimers consisting of a non-covalently associated alpha chain and beta chain, both of which are polymorphic. Class II MHC molecules present antigens that are internalized into vesicles, typically derived from extracellular microbes and soluble proteins. The class II beta 2 domain has a binding site for CD4, and therefore, the class II-peptide complex is recognized by CD4+ T cells, which are referred to as class II MHC-restricted because they can recognize antigens only in the context of self-class II molecules. The combination of HLA alleles in each individual is called the HLA haplotype.

Chronic prostatitis is a challenging diagnosis for many urologists, as men often present with perigenital pain, testicular pain, and prostatic pain exacerbated by sexual intercourse or pain that renders sexual intercourse impossible. Psychosexual dysfunction may be the underlying issue. The diagnosis of chronic prostatitis is based on the presence of persistent threads in voided urine and prostatic massage showing pus cells with or without bacteria in the absence of urinary infection.

The etiology of chronic prostatitis is thought to be the sequelae of inadequately treated acute prostatitis. Pus is often present in the prostatic secretion, and the responsible organism may be difficult to identify. Other organisms, such as Chlamydia species, may be responsible for chronic abacterial prostatitis.

The clinical features of chronic prostatitis are highly variable. Men with symptoms of posterior urethritis, prostatic pain, and perigenital pain accompanied by intermittent fever and pus cells or bacteria in the post-prostatic massage specimen should be diagnosed as having chronic prostatitis.

The diagnosis is valuable, as it can be confirmed by the three-glass urine test. If the first glass with the initial voided sample shows urine containing prostatic threads, prostatitis is present. Rectal examination of the prostate may be normal or may show a soft, boggy, and tender prostate. Examination of the prostatic fluid obtained by prostatic massage should show pus cells and bacteria. Urethroscopy may reveal inflammation of the prostatic urethra, and pus may be seen exuding from the prostatic ducts. The verumontanum is likely to be enlarged and oedematous.

Treatment should be administered only in accordance with bacteriological sensitivity tests. Antibiotics such as trimethoprim or ciprofloxacin may be effective. If Trichomonas or anaerobes are the responsible agent, metronidazole may be used. Treatment is typically continued for 10-12 weeks. If Chlamydia is suspected, doxycycline is the antibiotic treatment of choice. There is little evidence that prostatic massage helps in eradicating the infection.

The body's response to injury can be divided into three distinct phases: the Injury Phase, the Turning Point, and the Anabolic Phases.

The Injury Phase, also known as the phase of catabolism, begins at the time of injury and lasts for 2-5 days. During this phase, the body experiences hypermetabolism, characterized by increased levels of stress hormones such as cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon, as well as volume control hormones like renin-angiotensin, aldosterone, and ADH. This hormonal response leads to the breakdown of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates, resulting in proteolysis, lipolysis, and hyperglycemia. Despite the negative nitrogen balance, the body is able to initiate wound healing.

As the body begins to recover, a turning point is reached, marked physiologically by the shutdown of the neuroendocrine response and clinically by the appearance of getting well.

The Anabolic Phases, which follow the Injury Phase, are characterized by a gain in muscular strength or positive nitrogen balance in the Early Anabolic Phase. In the Late Anabolic Phase, the body experiences a gain in weight and body fat or positive caloric balance.

question: Treatment of choice for medullary carcinoma of thyroid is -
exp: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Total thyroidectomy Treatment of thyroid malignancies is as follows :- (Note- This is a very important and often repeated topic in PG exams, so if time permits one must turn the pages of Schwartz Sx or any other standard hook for detailed study).Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PCT)o High-risk tumors or bilateral tumorsTotal thyroidectomy (or near total thyroidectomy),o Low riskThe treatment is controversial.Conservative approach advocates hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy + isthmusectomy).More radical approach advocates total thyroidectomy (or near total thyroidectomy).Schwartz Sx and Devita's Oncology are in favour of radical approach.(High and Low risk decided by any one of the many classification systems)o If enlarged lymph nodes are foundModified radical neck dissection is done of the affected side.o When patients are found to have a minimal papillary thyroid carcinoma in a thyroid specimen removed for other reasons, unilateral thyroid lobectomy and isthmusectomy is usually considered to be adequate treatment, unless the tumor has evidence of angioinvasion, multifocality, or positive margins.Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC)o FNA biopsy is unable to distinguish benign follicular lesions from follicular carcinomas therefore, preoperative diagnosis of cancer is difficult unless distant metastases are present,o Patients diagnosed by FNA biopsy as follicular lesions should undergo thyroid lobectomy + isthmusectomy (because at least 80% of these patients will have benign adenomas).o The resected lobe is subjected to histology (intraoperative frozen - section examination, though usually not helpful should be performed in high risk cases).o If & follicular lesion larger than 4 cm is seen in an older patient - total thyroidectomy is done, because of high risk of cancer (50%) in this setting.o Prophylactic nodal dissection is not needed as nodal involvement is infrequent, but in the unusual patient with nodal metastases, therapeutic neck dissection is recommended.Lets also see what Sabiston 18/e p940 writes about treatment of Follicular lesions:The diagnosis of the carcinoma cannot be determined by preoperative FNA or intraoperative frozen section diagnosis of a follicular lesion.If the lesion is 2 cm or smaller and well contained within one thyroid lobe - thyroid lobectomy and isthmectomy.If the lesion is larger than 2 cm- total thyroidectomy.Medullary Thyroid Cancero Total Thyroidectomy is the treatment of choice for patients with MTC because of high incidence of multicentricity, the more aggressive course and RAI therapy usually being not effective,o The central compartment nodes are frequently involved early in the disease process, so that a bilateral central neck node dissection should be routinely performed. In patients with palpable cervical nodes or involved central neck nodes, ipsilateral or bilateral modified radical neck dissection is recommended. Similarly patient with tumors larger than 1 cm should undergo ipsilateral prophylactic modified radical neck dissection, because greater than 60% of these patients have nodal metastases. If ipsilateral nodes are positive, a contralateral node dissection should be performed.o In case of locally recurrent or metastatic disease, tumor debulking is advised, not only to ameliorate symptoms of flushing and diarrhoea, but also to decrease risk of death from recurrent central neck or mediastinal disease,o External beam radiotherapy is controversial, but is recommended for patients with unresectable residual or recurrent tumor. There is no effective chemotherapy regimeno If patients with MTC are found to have pheochromocytoma, this must be operated first.Anaplastic Carcinomao This tumor is one of the most aggressive thyroid malignancies, with few patients surviving six months beyond diagnosis.o All forms of treatment have been disappointing. If mass is resectable then thyroidectomy may lead to small improvement in survial.o Combined radiation and chemotherapy as adjuvant in resectable cases has been associated with prolonged survival. These are nowr also being used in neoadjuvant setting,o Tracheostomy may be needed to alleviate airway obstruction.

Breech Presentation

Breech presentation is a condition where the fetus presents its buttocks or feet instead of the head during delivery. The most common types of breech presentation are complete breech in multipara and frank breech (70%) in primi. Prematurity is the primary cause of breech presentation, followed by uterine malformations and hydrocephalus.

The sacrum serves as the denominator in breech presentation. The most common positions are sacroanterior, with left being the most common. The perinatal mortality rate for uncomplicated breech presentation is 3-10%. Foetal mortality is lowest in frank breech and highest in footling presentation.

Pelvic shape can influence the outcome of breech presentation. Gynaecoid and anthropoid pelvis are considered favourable for after coming head of breech. External cephalic version is an indication for after coming head of breech.

Placenta Previa

Placenta previa is a condition where the placenta is implanted wholly or partially in the lower uterine segment. Approximately 28% of women scanned before 24 weeks gestation have a low-lying placenta, with 3% at term. Trans-vaginal scanning improves the accuracy of diagnosing placenta previa, especially in cases of posterior placenta.

Placenta previa is classified into major and minor types. Major placenta previa occurs when the placenta encroaches or covers the internal cervical os, while minor placenta previa does not. This classification has replaced the previous grades I-IV.

Risk factors for placenta previa include increasing maternal age, smoking, previous caesarean section, and previous placenta previa, with a recurrence risk of 4-8%. Maternal risks associated with placenta previa include haemorrhage-related mortality, postpartum haemorrhage, complications of caesarean section, postpartum sepsis, and placenta accreta (up to 15% of placenta previa).

Fetal risks associated with placenta previa include prematurity, intrauterine growth restriction, congenital malformations (double risk of serious malformations), and mal-presentation.

Nitric oxide, also known as Endothelium-derived Relaxing Factor, is synthesized from the amino acid arginine by the enzyme nitric oxide synthase (NOS) in endothelial cells. This process occurs in the endothelial cells, which line the inner surface of blood vessels. Nitric oxide plays a crucial role in relaxing the smooth muscles of blood vessels, thereby causing vasodilation.

Additionally, the vasodilator nitroglycerin can also enter smooth muscle cells, where its metabolism leads to the formation of nitric oxide. This nitric oxide then activates the enzyme guanylate cyclase, which converts guanosine triphosphate (GTP) to cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). The increase in cGMP levels causes the relaxation of smooth muscle cells, ultimately leading to vasodilation.

There are three isoforms of NOS, each with distinct functions: neuronal NOS (nNOS), inducible NOS (iNOS), and endothelial NOS (eNOS).

exp_upd: Coical blindness, also known as visual evoked response (VER), assesses the functional state of the visual system beyond retinal ganglion cells. The clinically measured VER is primarily a response generated by the macula and optic nerve, as there is a disproportionately large projection of the macular area in the occipital cortex. Any abnormality in the macula, optic nerve, or the remaining optic pathway (beyond the optic nerve) can result in an increase in latency and a decrease in amplitude, or an extinguished response. The timing of the onset of the response, or latency, is a more reliable and generally more useful parameter than amplitude. question: All of the following are ominous signs in a case of severe head injury, EXCEPT:
exp: Anisocoria, decoicate posturing, and decerebrate posturing, all are mentioned as the ominous signs of severe head injury so development of diabetes insipidus is the answer of choice by exclusion here. Normally are equal in size, round and briskly reactive to light. Brain injury and pressure on the nerves leading to pupils can produce change in pupil size, shape and reacting to light and movement. These changes can be correlated with the severity and type of brain injury. A sudden enlargement (Dilation) of one pupil (anisocoria) is an ominous sighn that require immediate intervention. This typically signals increased pressure on one side of the brain, causing the brain to shift downwards in the skull cavity (uncal or tonsillar herniation). "While decoicate posturing is still an ominous sign of severe brain damage, decerebrate posturing is usually indicative of more severe damage as the rubrospinal tract and hence, the red nucleus, is also involved indicating lesion lower in the brainstem". Signs of brain injury: Loss of the normal autoregulation of blood pressure and pulse, called the cushing's reflex is a hallmark of severe brain injury or imminent crisis. This generally results in a sudden rise in blood pressure and a slowing of the pulse. A person with a moderate or severe TBI may have a headache that does not go away, repeated vomiting or nausea, convulsions, an inability to awaken, dilation of one or more pupils, slurred speech, aphasia (word- finding difficulties), dysahria (muscle weakness that causes disordered speech), weakness or numbness in the limbs, loss of coordination, confusion,restlessness, or agitation. When the pressure within the skull (intracranial pressure, abbreted ICP) rises too high, it can be deadly. Sign of Increased ICP include decreasing level of consciousness, paralysis or weakness on one side of the body, and a blown pupil, one that fail to constrict in response to light or is slow to do so. Cushing's triad, a slow hea rate with high blood pressure and respiratory depression is a classic manifestation of significantly raised ICP. Anisocoria, unequal pupil size is another sign of serious TBI. Abnormal posturing, a characteristic positioning of the limbs caused by severe diffuse injury or high ICP, is an ominous. Ref: Reddy 27/e, Page 213-25 ; Parikh 6/e, Page 4.92-110 ; Harrison 17/e, Page 2218

Glucose transporter-1 (GLUT-1) is a widely distributed protein that plays a crucial role in glucose transport across cell membranes. It is the most abundant glucose transporter in red blood cells (RBCs) and also serves as the major glucose transporter in the brain.

In addition to its presence in RBCs and the brain, GLUT-1 is also found in the placenta, where it facilitates glucose transport to the developing fetus. In contrast, GLUT-3 is primarily expressed in neurons, whereas GLUT-1 is not present in these cells.

Insulin-dependent glucose transporters, including GLUT-4, GLUT-8, and GLUT-12, are responsible for glucose uptake in certain tissues. GLUT-8, in particular, is also found in the blastocyst, a stage in embryonic development.

Finally, GLUT-9 is a urate transporter, responsible for the transport of uric acid in the body.

question: Tacrolimus acts by inhibiting:
exp: Tacrolimus (FK506) It is a newer immunosuppressant chemically different from cyclosporine, but having the same mechanism of action, and is -100 times more potent. It binds to a different cytoplasmic immunophilin protein labeled 'FKBP', but the subsequent steps are the same, i.e. inhibition of helper T cells calcineurin. Tacrolimus is administered orally as well as by i.v. infusion. Oral absorption is variable and decreased by food. It is metabolized by CYP3A4 Section 14 and excreted in bile with a longer tlh of 12 hour. It is paicularly valuable in liver transplantation because its absorption is not dependent on bile. Because of more potent action, it is also suitable for suppressing acute rejection that has set in. Hypeension, hirsutism and gum hyperplasia are less marked than cyclosporine, but tacrolimus is more likely to precipitate diabetes, cause neurotoxicity, alopecia, and diarrhea. ADPKD, the most common inheritable form of renal cystic disease, is characterized by the development of renal cysts. The disease can manifest at any age, including in utero, and typically becomes clinically apparent after age 30 years. Ninety-nine percent of affected individuals have a mutation in either the PKD1 gene on chromosome 16 or the PKD2 gene on chromosome 4. Sonographic identification of cysts is possible before age 20 years in almost all affected individuals.

ADPKD is associated with a high incidence of liver cysts, which increase with age. The signs and symptoms of ADPKD typically occur between the ages of 30 and 50 years and may include hematuria, flank pain, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal colic, and hypertension. Hepatic cysts are present in virtually all patients with ADPKD by age 50 years, although they are rarely symptomatic.

Intracranial aneurysms, also known as berry aneurysms, occur in 10% to 30% of patients with ADPKD, and approximately 9% of these patients die due to subarachnoid hemorrhages. Treatment options for ADPKD include tight blood pressure control, the use of ACE inhibitors and/or ARB BP medication, and the possible use of tolvaptan. Pain, often flank and/or abdominal, is the most common presenting symptom in adults, resulting from factors such as mass effect, bleeding into cysts, urinary tract infection, and nephrolithiasis. Hepatic cysts are the most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD, and other extra renal manifestations may include intracranial aneurysms, colonic diverticuli, mitral valve prolapse, and cysts in other organs.

question: If radius of a vessel is doubled then the blood flow is increased by?
exp: Ans. B 16 timesRef: Ganong: 26th ed. P 563* The influence of lumen diameter on resistance is dramatic. This is because resistance is inversely proportional to the radius of the blood vessel (one-half of the vessels diameter) raised to the fourth power (R=1/r4).* This means, that if an artery or arteriole constricts to one-half of its original radius, the resistance to flow will increase 16 times. And if an artery or arteriole dilates to twice its initial radius, then resistance in the vessel will decrease to 1/16 of its original value and flow will increase 16 times.

The maximum rate at which a solute can be transported, also known as the transport maximum (Tm), is limited by the saturation of the specific transport system. For the kidney, the Tm is less than the calculated value because not all nephrons have the same Tm, and some nephrons may excrete a substance before others have reached their Tm. The overall Tm of a substance for the kidney is reached when all nephrons have reached their capacity to reabsorb or secrete that substance.

For example, the Tm for glucose in a normal adult is approximately 375 milligrams per minute, whereas the filtered load is only 125 milligrams per minute (glomerular filtration rate x plasma glucose concentration). When the plasma glucose concentration rises above 200 milligrams per 100 milliliters (2 milligrams per milliliter), the filtered load exceeds the Tm, and excess glucose is not reabsorbed and appears in the urine. This is known as the renal threshold of glucose, which is the plasma level at which glucose first appears in the urine in more than the normal minute volumes.

Not all substances exhibit a transport maximum. Substances that are passively reabsorbed do not demonstrate a Tm, as their rate is determined by the electrochemical gradient, permeability, and time the solute remains within the tubule. Some actively transported substances also have an electrochemical gradient-time transport, such as sodium reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule. However, in the distal convoluted tubule, where the epithelium has tighter junctions and transports only small amounts of sodium, sodium reabsorption exhibits a Tm.

This can cause a range of symptoms, including shortness of breath, fatigue, and cyanosis (a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes). In severe cases, methemoglobinemia can lead to tissue hypoxia, organ failure, and even death. The condition is often caused by exposure to certain chemicals, such as aniline, and can be treated with methylene blue, a medication that helps to reduce the amount of methemoglobin in the blood.

question: Enzyme replacement therapy is available for all except:
exp: Ans- C San Philipo disease Ref= BACKGROUND: After many years of intensive investigation, enzyme-replacement therapy (ERT) has become standard treatment for patients with type 1 (non-neuronopathic) Gaucher's disease. ERT has greatly changed the clinical course of this disorder by reducing hepatosplenomegaly, by improving anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and by ameliorating skeletal damage. This example has prompted the investigation of ERT for several other metabolic disorders. The results of several of these trials have recently been published. RECENT DEVELOPMENTS: In addition to Gaucher's disease, the effects of ERT in four other major metabolic storage disorders have been reported. Among these rare orphan diseases are Fabry's disease, in which the heart, kidney, gastrointestinal tract, and peripheral nerves are damaged; Pompe's disease, in which the heart, skeletal muscles, and brain are involved; Hurler's disease and Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome in which the eyes, liver, joints, and skeleton are usually affected. Responses to ERT in these four disorders have generally been encouraging although the degree and extent of benefit vary considerably. WHERE NEXT: There are several critical features of ERT that require attention and amelioration. Among these are the development of severity-score indices that can be used to explicitly quantify the benefit of ERT. The benefit of this treatment has been slight in Fabry's disease and is yet to be fully shown in the other three disorders. Secondly, novel technologies need to be developed to deliver therapeutic enzymes effectively to tissues such as the cardiac muscle and kidney in Fabry's disease, skeletal muscle in patients with Pompe's disease, and to joint tissues and structures in patients with Hurler's disease and Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome. Finally, an all-encompassing concern is to devise methods to ameliorate the damage to the central and peripheral nervous systems that occurs in specific phenotypes of these disorders. In this review we descibe emerging strategies that seem to be useful in these critical regards.

The spherocytes of Hereditary Spherocytosis have two primary defects: reduced deformability and reduced membrane plasticity. On a peripheral smear, these spherocytes appear as small, irregularly shaped cells with a characteristic lack of central pallor. question: Test performed to compare weight of lung to body weight is?
exp: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Ploucquet's Test Tests used in infanticide Ploucquet's test: o Weight of lung is measured in relation to body wieght. Before birth weight of lung is 1/70 of body weight and after respiration it becomes 1/35 of body weight due to increased blood flow in lung beds. Static test or Fodere's test: o The average weight of both lungs before respiration is 30-40 gm and after respiration is 60-70 cm. Hydrostatic test (Raygat's test, 1st life test): o The specific gravity of a non-respired lung is 1040-1050 and of a respired lung is 940-950, so, after respiration lung floats on water (specific gravity of water is 1000). o False positive hydrostatic test may occur (i.e.non-respired lung may float) in decomposition and in attempted artificial respiration. o False negative hydrostatic test (i.e. respired lung may sink down) may occur in atelectasis, pulmonary oedema, bronchopneumonia, and congenital syphylis. Breslau's second life test: o It assumes that a live born child would respire and therefore, would also swallow some air into the stomach and bowel. o Hence they float on water. This test is falsely positive in putrefaction (due to putrefied gases) or in cases of attempted artificial respiration. Werdin's test: o Before birth middle ear contains gelatinous embryonic tissue which is replaced by air after respiration.

exp_upd:
Ploucquet's Test is used to determine whether a newborn has been breathing or not. The test involves measuring the weight of the lung in relation to the body weight. Before birth, the weight of the lung is approximately 1/70 of the body weight, while after respiration, it becomes 1/35 of the body weight due to increased blood flow in the lung beds.

The static test, also known as Fodere's test, involves measuring the average weight of both lungs before and after respiration. Typically, the weight of the lungs before respiration is between 30-40 grams, while after respiration, it is between 60-70 grams.

The hydrostatic test, also known as Raygat's test or the first life test, involves determining the specific gravity of the lung. Before respiration, the specific gravity of the lung is typically between 1040-1050, while after respiration, it is between 940-950. This means that after respiration, the lung will float on water, which has a specific gravity of 1000. However, false positive results may occur in cases of decomposition or attempted artificial respiration, while false negative results may occur in cases of atelectasis, pulmonary edema, bronchopneumonia, and congenital syphilis.

Breslau's second life test assumes that a live-born child would breathe and therefore swallow some air into the stomach and bowel, causing the child to float on water. This test is falsely positive in cases of putrefaction or attempted artificial respiration.

Werdin's test involves examining the middle ear, which contains gelatinous embryonic tissue before birth. After respiration, the middle ear is filled with air.

Osteosarcoma is a rare long-term complication of Paget's disease. Paget's disease can lead to various complications, including osseous deformities, fractures, osteoahrosis, basilar impression, spinal stenosis, and neurologic abnormalities. Less commonly encountered complications include bone tumors, soft-tissue masses, osteomyelitis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, rheumatoid arthritis and its variants, and crystal deposition disease.

One common complication of Paget's disease is osteoahrosis, which results from altered biomechanics across grossly abnormal bones and joints, leading to cailaginous and osseous degeneration. The hip and knee are the joints most frequently affected. The pattern of narrowing of the articular space in Paget's disease differs from that in primary degenerative joint disease. ATP synthesis in the electron transport chain (ETC) occurs through the enzyme F0F1 ATPase, also known as ATPase synthase. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of ADP to ATP. The free energy of electron transport is conserved by pumping protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space, creating an electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. The outer side of the membrane becomes positively charged compared to the inside.

The electrochemical potential of this gradient is used to synthesize ATP by ATPase synthase. The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to protons, so proton pumps are required to pump protons (hydrogen ions) from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space. The complexes IQ (Site I), IIIQ (Site II), and IVQ (Site III) act as proton pumps, ejecting protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space.

Complex I (NADH-CoQ reductase) and complex III (CoQ-cytochrome c reductase) pump 4 protons each, while complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) pumps 2 protons. The concentration of hydrogen ions (protons) on the outer side of the inner membrane becomes higher compared to the inner side, resulting in the generation of the electrochemical potential, or proton motive force.

Due to this electrochemical potential, the H+ ions ejected out by the proton pumps flow back into the mitochondrial matrix down its electrochemical gradient through the F0F1 ATPase molecule, also known as complex V of the respiratory chain. This proton influx causes ATP synthesis. The F0 component acts as a channel for the passage of hydrogen ions, while the F1 component possesses ATP synthase activity, which is switched on when the hydrogen ions pass through the F0 component.

As a result, phenylalanine is not converted into tyrosine, making tyrosine an essential amino acid. This metabolic shift leads to an accumulation of phenylalanine, phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, and phenyl-lactate in the body.

The primary symptom of untreated PKU is mental retardation, which is a result of consuming foods that contain phenylalanine, a toxic substance to brain tissue. Babies with PKU are typically normal at birth but may present with vomiting, followed by gradual development of mental retardation and growth retardation. Other characteristic features include light complexion, blue iris, microcephaly, rash, hypertonia, seizures, exaggerated tendon reflex, wide-spaced teeth, enamel hypoplasia, and hyperactivity. Additionally, individuals with PKU often exhibit a musty or mousy odor in their urine and other body secretions due to the presence of phenylketones.

Essential fatty acids (EFAs) are three polyunsaturated fatty acids: linoleic acid, linolenic acid, and arachidonic acid. These EFAs cannot be synthesized in the body and must be provided through the diet. A deficiency in EFAs can lead to growth retardation and other deficiency symptoms.

Linoleic acid is the most important EFA, as it can be converted into arachidonic acid through a three-stage reaction involving acetyl-CoA and pyridoxal phosphate. Arachidonic acid is a biologically important precursor for the synthesis of prostaglandins and leukotrienes in the body.

EFAs play a crucial role in various bodily functions, including:

* Structural elements of tissues: EFAs occur in higher concentrations in lipids associated with structural elements of tissues.
* Synthesis of prostaglandins and other compounds: Prostaglandins are synthesized from arachidonic acid by the cyclooxygenase enzyme system, while leukotrienes are formed from arachidonic acid in leucocytes by the lipoxygenase pathway.
* Structural element of mitochondrial membrane: A deficiency in EFAs can cause swelling of the mitochondrial membrane, leading to a reduction in the efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation.
* Serum level of cholesterol: Fats with high concentrations of polyunsaturated fatty acids tend to lower serum levels of cholesterol.
* Effect on clotting time: Prolongation of clotting time is noted in the ingestion of fats rich in EFAs.
* Effect on fibrinolytic activity: An increase in fibrinolytic activity follows the ingestion of fats rich in EFAs.
* Role in fatty liver: Deficiency in EFAs produces fatty liver.
* Role in vision: Docosahexaenoic acid, formed from dietary linolenic acid, enhances the electrical response of photoreceptors to illumination, making linolenic acid necessary for optimal vision.

A deficiency in EFAs has not been unequivocally demonstrated in humans, but symptoms of EFA deficiency can be produced in weaning animals. Deficiency manifestations include cessation of growth, skin lesions, abnormalities of pregnancy and lactation in adult females, fatty liver, and kidney damage.

Some cases of eczema-like dermatitis, degenerative changes in arterial walls, and fatty liver in humans may be due to EFA deficiency. Administration of EFAs in such cases has been reported to produce some improvement in eczema in children, prevent fatty liver, and lower cholesterol levels. Infants and babies with low-fat diets may develop typical skin lesions that can be improved with EFA supplementation.

question: I.R.I.S. is:
exp: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome o The term "immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome" (IRIS) describes a collection of inflammatory disorders associated with paradoxical worsening of preexisting infectious processes following the initiation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in HIV-infected individuals. Preexisting infections in individuals with IRIS may have been previously diagnosed and treated or they may be subclinical and later unmasked by the host's regained capacity to mount an inflammatory response.o If immune function improves rapidly following the commencement of HAART, systemic or local inflammatory reactions may occur at the site or sites of the preexisting infection.o This inflammatory> reaction is usually self-limited, especially if the preexisting infection is effectively treated. However, long-term sequelae and fatal outcomes may rarely occur, particularly when neurologic structures are involved.Diagnostic criteria for IRISo There is no universally agreed-upon definition for IRIS. However, it is generally accepted that the diagnosis of IRIS requires the worsening of a recognized (''paradoxical" IRIS) or unrecognized pre-existing infection ("unmasking" IRIS) in the setting of improving immunologic function.Most or all of the following features should be present in order to make the diagnosis:o The presence of AIDS with a low pretreatment CD4 count (often less than 100 cells/microL). One important exception to this general rule is tuberculosis. IRIS secondary to preexisting M. tuberculosis infection may occur in individuals with CD4 counts >200.o A positive virologic and immunological response to ART.o The absence of evidence of drug-resistant infection, bacterial superinfection, drug allergy or other adverse drug reactions, patient noncompliance, or reduced drug levels due to drug-drug interactions or malabsorption after appropriate evaluation for the clinical presentation.o The presence of clinical manifestations consistent with an inflammatory condition.o A temporal association between HAART initiation and the onset of clinical features of illness.Summary and recommendationso The clinical features of each individual case of IRIS are highly variable and data from controlled trials have not been published thus far to provide clear guidelines. Our recommendations are based on clinical experience, case reports, case series, and expert opinion:# Although it is reasonable to perform studies looking for unmasked subclinical opportunistic infection, the diagnosis of IRIS is generally one of exclusion. Investigations to rule out the possibility of drug reaction, patient noncompliance, persistently active infection and/or drug resistance are usually warranted before concluding that IRIS is present.# Most patients with IRIS develop symptoms within one week to a few months after the initiation of HAART. With later onset, other diagnoses become more likely. Abacavir hypersensitivity can be confused with IRIS, but symptoms worsen soon after each dose of abacavir. The diagnostic work-up for abacavir hypersensitivity reaction includes genetic testing for HLA-B5701.# When a diagnosis of IRIS is considered highly likely, further or repeated invasive diagnostic procedures to locate an occult infection may be reasonably delayed, deferred, or altogether avoided.# Treatment for the underlying pathogen should generally be started or continued in patients who develop IRIS. This is particularly important when treating patients with IRIS associated with hepatitis B virus.# Corticosteroids or NSAIDS may help decrease the inflammatory response in some patients with IRIS. The decision to use corticosteroids should be individualized and should take into account the risks of therapy. When we choose to treat with corticosteroids, we initiate therapy with prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg/day (maximal dose 60 to 80 mg) and then taper steroid therapy while monitoring for recurrence of clinical symptoms over the ensuing weeks to months.# For most patients, we suggest initiation of ART within two weeks of starting treatment of the underlying opportunistic infection to decrease the risk of clinical progression of AIDS and death.# For OIs that lack proven effective therapies other than HAART (eg, PML), we believe it is best to treat these patients with HAART despite the risk of an adverse outcome. We normally do not use steroids in such patients unless or until symptoms of IRIS appear.

question: Dose response relationship is a measure of
exp: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Strength of association* Likehood of a causal relationship is increased by the presence of the following criteria :1. Temporal association# It implies that suspected cause preceds the observed effect. It is the most important criteria.2. Strength of association# It implies how strongly exposure is associated with disease. It can be determined by relative risk (in cohort study), odds ratio (in case-control study), dose response relationship. and cessation of exposure (reversibility).3. Consistency of association# The association is consistent if the results are replicated when studies in different settings and by different methods.4. Coherence of association# The causal association must be coherent (supported by) with relevant facts.5. Specificity of association# It is implies a 'one to one relationship'. It is the weakest and the most difficult criteria to establish.6. Biological plausibility# It implies biological credibility to the association, that is the association agrees with current understanding of the response of cells, tissues organs and system to stimuli.# For example, positive association of food intake with GI cancer is biological plausable (food enters GIT and causes cellular response), while positive association of food intake and skin cancer is not biological plausible.

Mifepristone is an orally active glucocorticoid receptor blocker with antiglucocorticoid, antiandrogenic, and potent competitive anti-progesterone activity. It is a steroid with an affinity for progesterone receptors. A single dose of 600 mg or 25 mg taken twice daily for four days can induce abortion in cases of amenorrhea lasting more than 48 hours. Although mifepristone does not prevent fertilization, it blocks the action of progesterone on the endometrium, causing sloughing and shedding of deciduas, which leads to abortion. However, the emptying of the uterus is often incomplete, and surgical evacuation is typically necessary.

The addition of prostaglandin (Misoprostol) on the last day of treatment can improve the rate of complete abortion. Mifepristone is metabolized by CYP 3A4, and its activity can be affected by inhibitors such as erythromycin and ketoconazole, as well as inducers like rifampicin and anticonvulsants.

Mifepristone has several uses, including the termination of pregnancy, cervical ripening, postcoital contraception, and the induction of labor. It can also be used to treat Cushing syndrome and is being evaluated for the treatment of endometriosis, uterine fibroids, breast cancer, and meningioma. Common side effects of mifepristone include anorexia, nausea, tiredness, abdominal discomfort, uterine cramps, and loose stools.

Phenoxybenzamine is a pharmacological treatment used to control blood pressure in patients with pheochromocytoma, particularly when the tumor cannot be removed or before surgery. This medication works by blocking alpha-adrenoreceptors, which reverses peripheral vasoconstriction and helps to lower blood pressure. In hypertensive crises or intraoperative control of blood pressure, phentolamine is the medication of choice, with prazosin being an alternative option. Nitroprusside can also be used in certain situations.

In patients with adrenaline-secreting tumors, if tachycardia persists, a beta-blocker can be added after starting alpha-blockers. Additionally, ACE inhibitors or calcium channel blockers may be used when blood pressure is difficult to control with phenoxybenzamine alone. Metyrosine has been used with some success to block catecholamine synthesis in malignant pheochromocytoma. Metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) is actively taken up by adrenergic tissue, and 123I-MIBG can be used for selective therapeutic irradiation of functioning metastases.

Hybridomas are cells that have been engineered to produce a specific antibody in large numbers. To achieve this, the qualities of two types of cells are combined: cells that can produce large amounts of pure antibody and cells that have the ability to grow continually. These two types of cells are then fused together to form a hybridoma.

The pure antibody-secreting cells are produced by injecting a specific antigen into a mouse and obtaining the antigen-specific plasma cells (antibody-producing cells) from the mouse's spleen. The cells that can grow indefinitely in culture are myeloma cells, which are cancerous cells. These two cell lines are fused together, and the hybrid cell produced can be cloned to produce large numbers of identical daughter clones. These daughter clone cells then produce antibodies. Since these antibodies come from only one type of cell (hybridoma cell), they are called monoclonal antibodies.

HAT (hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine) medium is used for the preparation of monoclonal antibodies because it allows only fused hybridoma cells to grow. It does not allow the unfused myeloma and unfused antibody cells to grow. This is because the medium is selective, allowing only the fused hybridoma cells to survive.

Purine synthesis is essential for the survival of cells. Purine can be synthesized in two ways: de novo synthesis, which requires the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme, and salvage pathway, which requires the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase enzyme. Myeloma cells lack the HGPRTase enzyme, so they cannot synthesize purine through the salvage pathway. Antibody cells, on the other hand, have the HGPRTase enzyme, so they can use the salvage pathway. Aminopterin inhibits the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme, which is essential for de novo synthesis of purine. When the two cell lines, antibody-producing cells and myeloma cells, are grown in HAT medium, only the fused hybridoma cells survive. Myeloma cells die because they lack the enzyme HGPRTase and cannot use the salvage pathway for purine synthesis. They also cannot use de novo synthesis, as aminopterin present in the HAT medium inhibits the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme. The unfused antibody-producing cells die because they cannot grow indefinitely due to their limited lifespan. Only the fused hybridoma cells grow indefinitely, as the antibody cell partner supplies HGPRTase, and the myeloma partner provides immortality (as it is a cancer cell).

The ventromedial part of the somites is called the sclerotome. The cells of the sclerotome migrate medially, surrounding the neural tube and giving rise to the vertebral column and ribs. The vertebral body may ossify from two primary centers, which soon fuse. In some cases, one of these centers may fail to develop, resulting in hemiveebrae, where only half of the body is present. The lateral part of the somite is called the dermatome, which gives rise to the dermis of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. The intermediate part of the somite is the myotome, which gives rise to striated muscle.

Additionally, common anomalies of the vertebral column include sacralization of L5, where the vertebral body is fused to the sacrum; lumbarization of S1, where it functions as a sixth lumbar vertebra; spondylolysis, where a bony defect develops between the pedicle and the lamina; and spondylolisthesis, where the vertebral body, pedicles, and superior facet joints slide anteriorly, leaving the posterior elements behind, most commonly occurring at L5.

Fungal (Mycotic) Corneal Ulcer:

Symptoms are much milder than the clinical signs. The ulcer appears dry-looking, grayish white, with elevated, rolled-out margins and feathery, finger-like extensions into the surrounding stroma under intact epithelium. A big hypopyon is often present, even if the ulcer is very small. Unlike bacterial ulcers, the hypopyon may not be sterile, as fungi can penetrate into the anterior chamber without perforation.

The ulcer is characterized by filamentous septate hyphae, producing multicellular fungi, most notably Fusarium and Aspergillus (fumigatus), which are common causative organisms in tropical and hot climates. Unicellular budding yeast, such as Candida, is the most common cause of fungal keratitis in temperate regions.

Predisposing factors include injury by vegetative materials or animal tail, excessive use of antibiotics, corneal trauma involving plant matter or gardening/agricultural tools, corneal disease, local immunosuppression, long-term use of topical steroids, prior corneal transplantation, contact lens wear, and diabetes mellitus.

Clinical features include marked ciliary and conjunctival congestion, with symptoms of pain, watering, and photophobia being disproportionately less. The ulcer may be accompanied by a sterile immune ring, multiple small satellite lesions, and a big hypopyon. Perforation is rare, and corneal vascularization is conspicuously absent.

Radiation-induced lung diseases, including radiation pneumonitis, are a well-known complication of therapeutic radiation of thoracic tumors, such as lung, esophageal, breast, and mediastinal cancers. Radiation pneumonitis can occur in both acute and chronic forms.

Acute radiation pneumonitis, also known as lymphocytic alveolitis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis, typically develops 1 to 6 months after irradiation, affecting 3% to 44% of patients, depending on the dose and age of the patient. Symptoms of acute radiation pneumonitis include fever, dyspnea out of proportion to the volume of lung irradiated, pleural effusion, and infiltrates that usually correspond to the area of previous irradiation. With steroid therapy, these symptoms may resolve completely in some patients, while in others, the condition may progress to chronic radiation pneumonitis.

Chronic radiation pneumonitis, also known as pulmonary fibrosis, is a consequence of the repair of injured endothelial and epithelial cells. It may also occur without antecedent pulmonary symptoms. Morphologic changes in chronic radiation pneumonitis include diffuse alveolar damage, characterized by severe atypia of hyperplastic type II cells and fibroblasts, as well as epithelial cell atypia and foam cells within vessel walls.

BNP analogues, such as Nesiritide, are typically used in the treatment of acute cardiac failure, but are not used in chronic therapy. In contrast, compensated heart failure, also known as chronic CHF, requires a different approach.

Digitalis, a Na+-K+ ATPase inhibitor, is often used in chronic CHF. By inhibiting Na+/K+ ATPase, digitalis exerts a positive inotropic effect on the heart, increasing its contractility. However, it does not act as a chronotropic agent, meaning it does not increase the workload on the heart, making it a useful treatment option for chronic conditions.

Aldosterone antagonists are also used in chronic CHF, as they have been shown to decrease morbidity and mortality. These medications are often used in combination with ACE inhibitors and ARBs to prevent cardiac remodeling.

Beta blockers, on the other hand, can precipitate acute decompensation of cardiac function and are therefore not typically used in acute cardiac failure. However, they are used in chronic CHF, as they have been shown to decrease mortality by reversing left ventricular hypertrophy.

Fungi can be classified based on their pathogenesis, which is the manner in which they cause disease in humans. Superficial mycoses, such as dermatophytosis, candidiasis, tinea, piedra, and pityriasis versicolor, affect the skin and its appendages. Cutaneous mycoses, like candidiasis, involve the skin, while subcutaneous mycoses, including mycotic mycetoma and chromoblastomycosis, affect the skin and underlying tissues. Rhinosporidiosis and sporotrichosis are examples of deep or systemic or visceral mycoses, which can affect various organs and tissues.

In addition to these categories, fungi can also be classified as opportunistic mycoses, such as mucor, aspergillus, candida, and penicillium, which cause disease in individuals with compromised immune systems. Mycotoxicoses, like those caused by aspergillus and claviceps purpura, involve the production of toxic compounds by fungi that can cause disease in humans.

Determinants of GFR include factors that increase or decrease glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, which in turn affect GFR. Glomerular hydrostatic pressure is determined by three variables: arterial pressure, afferent arteriolar resistance, and efferent arteriolar resistance.

Increased arterial pressure tends to raise glomerular hydrostatic pressure and, therefore, increase GFR. Conversely, decreased arterial pressure, or hypotension, causes a decrease in GFR.

Afferent arteriolar constriction reduces glomerular hydrostatic pressure and decreases GFR, while dilation of the afferent arterioles increases both glomerular hydrostatic pressure and GFR.

Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic effect on GFR. Moderate constriction can lead to a slight increase in GFR, but severe constriction results in a decrease. Dilatation of the efferent arterioles decreases glomerular hydrostatic pressure and, therefore, decreases GFR.

Increased glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure decreases GFR, while decreased colloid osmotic pressure increases GFR. For example, in hypoproteinemia, decreased colloid osmotic pressure can lead to an increase in GFR.

Increased renal blood flow increases GFR by decreasing glomerular capillary oncotic pressure. This occurs because increased RBF causes a decrease in filtration fraction, resulting in more fluid remaining in the glomerular capillary and dilution of plasma proteins, which in turn decreases oncotic pressure.

Conversely, decreased renal blood flow decreases GFR. Increased Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure, resulting from increased tubular hydrostatic pressure due to obstruction, also decreases GFR.

A decrease in glomerular capillary filtration coefficient (Kf) decreases GFR. Kf depends on the permeability of the glomerular membrane as well as its surface area. Increased thickness of the membrane decreases permeability and Kf, which can occur in conditions such as chronic hypertension and diabetes.

Kf can be altered by mesangial cells, which contract and cause a decrease in Kf by decreasing the surface area of the membrane. Relaxation of mesangial cells increases Kf. Contraction of mesangial cells, resulting in decreased GFR, is produced by various factors, including endothelin, angiotensin II, vasopressin, norepinephrine, PAF, PDGF, thromboxane A, PGF2, leukotrienes C4 and D4, and histamine. Relaxation of mesangial cells, resulting in increased GFR, is produced by factors such as ANP, dopamine, PGE2, and cAMP.

Ulnar Nerve Lesion

I. Lesion at the Elbow

Cubital tunnel syndrome is a condition characterized by compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow. When the nerve is severely compressed, it can cause wasting of the muscles on the medial side of the forearm, including those responsible for flexion of the fourth and fifth fingers. Weakness of flexion is evident when the proximal portions of these fingers are held steady, making it impossible to flex the terminal phalanges. The hypothenar muscles, which control abduction of the fifth finger, are also paralyzed, leading to an inability to abduct this finger. The interossei and medial two lumbricals, responsible for the "claw hand" deformity, are also affected. Wasting of the hypothenar muscles, interossei, and medial portion of the thenar eminence may occur. Additionally, there is weakness in movement of the fingers and abduction of the extended thumb against the palm. Sensory loss is observed on the dorsal and palmar aspects of the medial side of the hand, as well as the medial one and a half fingers.

II. Lesion at the Wrist

When the ulnar nerve is compressed at the wrist, cutaneous sensation of the hand and fingers is often spared. However, if the lesion is proximal to the wrist, it can cause impaired sensation on the palmar aspects of the hand and the fourth and fifth fingers, as well as muscle weakness, particularly in the hypothenar eminence. The adductor pollicis, supplied by the median nerve, is also affected, leading to the use of the flexor pollicis longus to hold objects. This is evident in the "book test" or Froment sign. Percussion over the ulnar nerve at the wrist can elicit a positive Tinel's sign, characterized by a sensation of "pins and needles" in the distribution of the nerve, including the ulnar side of the hand and the fourth and fifth fingers. A positive Phalen's test is also observed, with paraesthesias in the fourth and fifth fingers, which can be elicited by holding the wrist in maximum flexion for 30-60 seconds.

The first class of antidepressant drugs introduced was the monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs). These medications work by inhibiting the enzyme monoamine oxidase, which degrades three important neurotransmitters: dopamine, adrenaline, and serotonin. By blocking this enzyme, MAOIs allow these neurotransmitters to accumulate in the brain, increasing their levels.

MAOIs are used to treat atypical depression and depression with reverse vegetative symptoms. However, they can have significant side effects, including hypertensive crisis and the "cheese reaction." The latter occurs when a patient taking an MAOI consumes tyramine-rich foods, such as aged cheese or fermented foods. This can lead to an excessive release of monoamines, which cannot be degraded by the blocked enzyme, resulting in a hypertensive crisis.

Common side effects of MAOIs include paresthesias, which can be caused by pyridoxine deficiency, as well as weight gain and sexual dysfunction.

Alport's syndrome is a hereditary nephritis characterized by microscopic hematuria, which is often the first symptom. The condition is also associated with deafness. The pathology of Alport's syndrome is characterized by diffuse glomerular basement membrane thickening. The basement membrane of the glomerulus is composed of type IV collagen, which is made up of six different chains: a1 and a2 located on chromosome 13, a3 and a4 located on chromosome 2, and a5 and a6 located on chromosome 6. The a3, a4, and a5 chains form a collagen network present in the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea, and lens capsule.

These mutations are heterogeneous and affect all domains of the a5 chain. As a result, the glomerular membrane is thin, and electron microscopy demonstrates irregular foci of thickening alternating with thinning, often with a "basket weave appearance."

ECG is essential in diagnosing hyperkalemia in the appropriate clinical setting. ECG changes have a sequential progression of effects, which roughly correlate with the potassium level. The early changes of hyperkalemia include peaked T waves, shortened QT interval, and ST-segment depression. These changes are followed by bundle-branch blocks, causing a widening of the QRS complex, increases in the PR interval, and decreased amplitude of the P wave. With appropriate treatment, these changes reverse. If left untreated, the P wave eventually disappears, and the QRS morphology widens to resemble a sine wave. Ventricular fibrillation or asystole may follow. ECG findings generally correlate with the potassium level, but potentially life-threatening arrhythmias can occur without warning at almost any level of hyperkalemia.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a clonal histiocytic disorder characterized by the presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm of Langerhans cells. These granules are visible under electron microscopy, appearing as a "Tennis racquet" shape. LCH cells also express enzymes such as a-Naphthyl Acetate Esterase, a-Naphthyl Butyrate Esterase, and Acid Phosphatase, as well as markers like S-100, CD1a, and HLA-DR.

LCH can present in three clinicopathological entities: acute disseminated LCH, multifocal LCH, and unifocal LCH. Acute disseminated LCH, also known as Letterer-Siwe disease, typically affects children under the age of 2 years and is characterized by a seborrhoeic-type skin rash, moderate hepatomegaly, few palpable lymph nodes, and pulmonary lesions. Bone lesions are common, with over 80% of cases showing lytic lesions. Fever, otitis media, and mastoiditis may also occur, and CNS involvement can result from contiguous spread. Hematologic findings may include pancytopenia, with bone marrow infiltration by histiocytes.

Multifocal LCH involves multiple systems and has a better prognosis than acute disseminated LCH. It is characterized by fever, rash, and involvement of the posterior pituitary, which can lead to diabetes insipidus. Hand-Schuller-Christian disease is a rare variant of multifocal LCH, featuring a triad of exophthalmos, diabetes insipidus, and calvarial defect.

Unifocal LCH, on the other hand, presents as a focal lytic lesion in the bone, with an excellent prognosis.

The cervix contains more fibrous tissue and collagen than muscle fibers, with collagen making up approximately 90% of its composition. In contrast, muscle fibers account for only about 10% of the cervix. During late pregnancy and at term, the hormone prostaglandin plays a crucial role in breaking down collagen into a fluid form, allowing the cervix to become soft and pliable, facilitating labor.

In early pregnancy, increased vascularity within the cervix's stroma beneath the epithelium can create an ectocervical blue tint, known as Chadwick's sign. Additionally, cervical edema can lead to the softening of the cervix, a phenomenon referred to as Goodell's sign. The softening of the cervix's isthmus is another significant indicator, known as Hegar's sign.

question: Specific reason to disallow the sample for culture
exp: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Sample brought in formalin Guidelines for proper specimen collection 1) Collect specimen before administering antibiotics or antivirals when possible. 2) Collect specimen with as little skin contamination as possible to ensure that the sample collected represents the infected site. 3) Utilize appropriate collection devices. Use sterile equipment and aseptic technique to collect specimens to prevent introduction of microorganisms during invasive procedures. 4) Clearly label the specimen container with patient's name, hospital number or other identifying number (i.e. bih date, requisition number), date and time of collection. 5) Collect an adequate amount of specimen. Inadequate amounts of specimen may yield false-negative results. 6) If a specimen is collected through intact skin, cleanse the skin first. For example, use 70% alcohol followed by iodine solution (1 to 2% tincture of iodine or 10% solution of povidone iodine). 7) Collect fluid specimens in sturdy, sterile, screw cap, leak proof containers with lids that do not create an aerosol when opened. Specimens obtained by a physician using needle aspiration should be transferred to a sterile tube or anaerobi transpo l prior to transpo of the specimen to the laboratory. If there is little material in the syringe, the physician should draw a small amount of sterile nonbacteriostatic 0.85% NaCI through the syringe and then transfer the specimen to a sterile tube. Alternatively, and ONLY if the specimen will be compromised by transferring it from the syringe, a small amount of sterile 0.85% NaCI may be drawn into the syringe prior to removal of the needle. DO NOT TRANSPO SYRINGES WITH NEEDLES ATTACHED AND/OR RECAPPED. Attach syringe cap ONLY if necessary. The physician should use a protective device while removing the needle to avoid injury and should cap the syringe with a sterile cap prior to transpoing it to the laboratory. 9) Any Micorbiology and Virology specimens collected in formalin are UNACCEPTABLE for culture.

Teratomas are classified into three categories: mature (benign), monodermal or specialized, and immature (malignant).

Mature (benign) teratomas are cystic and known as dermoid cysts. These neoplasms are thought to arise from the ectodermal differentiation of totipotential cells. They are bilateral in 10% to 15% of cases. Characteristically, they are unilocular cysts containing hair and cheesy sebaceous material. On section, they reveal a thin wall lined by an opaque, grey-white, wrinkled, apparent epidermis. A solid prominence, known as Rokitansky's protuberance, is often seen, containing tissue elements such as tooth, bone, cartilage, and various other odd tissues. The cyst wall is composed of stratified squamous epithelium with underlying sebaceous glands, hair shafts, and other skin adnexal structures. In most cases, structures from other germ layers can be identified, including cartilage, bone, thyroid tissue, and other organoid formations. In rare instances, dermoids may be incorporated within the wall of a mucinous cystadenoma. About 1% of dermoids undergo malignant transformation, typically involving squamous cell carcinoma.

Monodermal or specialized teratomas are rare tumors that include struma ovarii and carcinoid. These tumors are always unilateral, although a contralateral teratoma may be present. Struma ovarii is composed entirely of mature thyroid tissue and may hyperfunction, causing hyperthyroidism. The ovarian carcinoid, which likely arises from intestinal epithelium in a teratoma, may produce 5-hydroxytryptamine and the carcinoid syndrome, particularly in large tumors.

Immature (malignant) teratomas are rare tumors that differ from benign teratomas in that the component tissue resembles that observed in the fetus or embryo rather than in the adult. These tumors are typically found in prepubertal adolescents and young women and grow rapidly, frequently penetrating the capsule with local spread or metastases. On microscopy, varying amounts of immature tissue are present, differentiating toward cartilage, glands, bone, muscle, nerve, and others. The histologic grade of the tumor, based on the proportion of tissue containing immature neuroepithelium, is an important risk factor for extraovarian spread.

Pityriasis rosacea, also known as P. rosea, is a common scaly disorder that typically affects children and young adults between the ages of 10 and 35 years. The condition is characterized by the appearance of round or oval, pink-brown patches with a superficial, centrifugal scale, often distributed over the trunk in a Christmas tree pattern. P. rosea is thought to be a viral disease, and while the exact etiology is not fully understood, Human Herpes virus 6 (HHV 6) and Human Herpes virus 7 (HHV 7) may play a role.

The clinical manifestations of P. rosea typically begin with an upper respiratory prodrome or a mild flu. One to two weeks later, an annular erythematous plaque appears on the trunk, often referred to as the "mother patch" or "herald patch." Over the next one to two weeks, fresh patches appear all over the trunk, often in a Christmas tree or fir tree configuration. The lesions are typically pinkish on white skin, earning the name "rosea." However, on dark Indian skin, the lesions may appear skin-colored or brown.

A key diagnostic clue is the presence of a fine scale at the edge of the lesion, referred to as centrifugal scale, collarette scales, or cigarette paper scales. Lesions typically subside with hyperpigmentation. While the trunk is the most commonly affected area, in approximately 20% of cases, lesions may occur predominantly on the extremities and neck, known as an inverse pattern.

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a hormonal disorder characterized by high levels of prolactin. The condition is often accompanied by amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhea, obesity, hirsutism, and infertility. The classic Stein-Leventhal triad consists of anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and obesity.

The ovaries are typically enlarged and covered with a thick, smooth fibrotic pearly white capsule. Long-term complications of PCOS include hyperplasia of the endometrium, cardiovascular disease, and non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM).

Laboratory tests often reveal raised LH levels, a high LH/FSH ratio (typically 3:1), and increased androgens. Estrogen levels may be high or normal, and progesterone is typically absent. Treatment options for PCOS include clomiphene citrate, which is often used to induce ovulation in women seeking pregnancy. Folliculogenesis can be monitored using ultrasound. For hirsutism associated with PCOS, GnRH analogues may be tried.

The most common benign tumor of the liver is a type of hemangioma. These tumors are more commonly seen in women, typically at the age of 45. Hemangiomas are classified into two main categories: small capillary hemangiomas, which have no clinical significance, and larger cavernous hemangiomas. Laboratory tests, such as liver function tests and tumor markers, are typically normal. Diagnosis is typically made radiologically, using computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, which can detect a typical peripheral nodular enhancement pattern. Percutaneous biopsy is not recommended due to its potential danger and inaccuracy.
