Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by a loss of bone mass. It is essential to note that the mineralization of the bone remains normal. This loss of bone mass increases the likelihood of fracture with age. Elderly women are at a higher risk of osteoporosis due to the accelerated loss of bone mass following menopause, compared to men. Several risk factors contribute to the development of osteoporosis, including Caucasian and Asian ethnicity, female sex, increasing age, early menopause, smoking, excess alcohol consumption, coicosteroid use, hypogonadism, and rheumatoid arthritis.

The reduced bone mass associated with osteoporosis can lead to vertebral crush fractures, most of which are asymptomatic. The extent of osteoporosis is best evaluated using a dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan, which provides a T score. This score represents the number of standard deviations the patient's bone mineral density differs from the population average for a young healthy adult. The World Health Organization defines osteoporosis as a T score of -2.5 or greater, indicating a bone mineral density more than 2.5 standard deviations below that of a young healthy adult. A T score between -1.5 and -2.5 is classified as osteopenia.

Spinal x-rays are useful for assessing vertebral crush fractures but cannot evaluate the extent of osteoporosis. Full blood count, bone, and liver biochemistry tests are not affected by osteoporosis. Treatment options for osteoporosis include the use of bisphosphonates, hormone replacement therapy, and raloxifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator.

question: In nonunion of scaphoid vescularized muscle pedicle graft is taken from.
exp: C i.e. Pronator quadrates Blood supply of scaphoid enters distally mainly through the dorsal ridge (spiral groove, narrow non aicular region in the waist) and proximal segment is supplied by retrograde intraosseous blood flow from distal to proximal. This unusual pattern of vascularity is responsible for higher probability of nonunion & avascular necrosis of proximal fragment in fractures of scaphoid. Therefore 0-1% of distal third, 20% of middle third, 40% of proximal third and 100% of proximal pole fractures result in AVN and nonunion. Scaphoid Fracture Functional Anatomy & Epidemiology Scaphoid is the most commonly fractured bone in the - carpusQ, in adult as well as children. However unlike in adults and adolescents, the fracture is rare in young children. (d/t cailagenous nature of carpal bones in children) Scaphoid fracture is seen most commonly in males between the ages of 15 and 30. (adolscents & adults)Q - Scaphoid may be divided into proximal, middle and distal thirds. The middle third is termed the waist. The scaphoid tubercle forms the distal volar prominence. Middle third (Waist) fractures are most commonQ accounting for - 70% of scaphoid fractures > proximal pole fracture (20%) > distal pole fracture (10%), in adults & adolescents. Investigation Distal pole avulsion type fracture is most common fracture type in children Q. Anteroposterior, lateral and oblique views are all essential; often a recent fracture shown only in the oblique viewQ. So a routine scaphoid x- ray series must include:- Radial and ulnar deton PA views with the wrist in about 30deg of extension (by asking to make a fist gently) True lateral view Radial oblique (supinated PA) view and ulnar oblique (pronated PA) view. Comparison view of opposite wrist. However it is common for the fracture not to be visible on the initial films. If doubt exists, the scaphoid should be immobilized in plaster and repeat radiograph obtained in 1421 days as the late films are usually positiveQ. Bone scan, trispiral tomography are other investigations ; occult scaphoid fractures can be reliably diagnosed by MRI & nucleotide scan. Vascularity, Nonunion & AVN Blood supply of scaphoid is precarious. It receives most of its blood supply from two major vascular pedicles (dorsal & volar branches) from the radial aery, both entering distallyQ. Volar (palmar) scaphoid branch of radial aery enters the scaphoid tubercle and supplies its distal 20-30%. Dorsal scaphoid branch of radial aery enters through numerous small foramina along the spiral groove & dorsal ridge and account for 80% of its blood supply. There is usually no or rarely a single perforater proximal to the waist of scaphoid. Hence vascularity of proximal fragment is maintained by retrograde intraosseous blood flow from distal to proximal; 7080% of which is provided by dorsal branch. The distal scaphoid has a dense vascular network whereas intraosseous vascular density declines proximally, leaving the proximal pole with sparse blood supply. Because of this unusual retrograde vascular supply to proximal segment, the scaphoid has a high risk of nonunion and AVN after fracture through waist and proximal pole. Because the scaphoid aiculates with four carpal bones & radius, most of its surface is composed of aicular cailage. Therefore, the vascular supply comes through -a narrow non aicular region in the waist. Most of the blood supply to the scaphoid enters distally, so blood supply of scaphoid diminishes proximallyQ. This accounts for the fact that 1% of distal third, 20% of middle third, 40% of proximal third and 100% of proximal pole fractures result in avascular necrosis or non union of the proximal fragment2. -Because it aiculates with distal radius, and with 4 of remaining 7 carpal bones, the scaphoid moves with nearly all carpal motions, especially volar flexion. Any alteration of its aicular surface through fracture, dislocation, or subluxation or any change of its stability by ligamentous rupture can cause severe secondary changes throughout the entire carpus. Management Stable and undisplaced fractures are treated by scaphoid cast immobilization (glass holding dorsal and radial flexion positionQ impacts the scaphoid fragments and minimises the shearing effects), for 4 - 8 weeks in distal third, 6 - 12 weeks in middle third and 12- 20 weeks in proximal third fractures. Scaphoid cast is applied from the upper forearm to just sho of meta carpophalyngeal joints of fingers, but incorporating proximal phalynx of thumb. The wrist is held dorsiflexed and the thumb forwards in "glass holding position" - A displaced fracture, by definition, is one with > 1 mm of step-off or >60degof scapholunate or >15deg of lunato- capitate angulation. The subtle signs of displacement or instability are - opening & obliquity of fracture line, angulation of distal fragment, and fore shoening of scaphoid image. Displaced- unstable fractures are treated by percutaneous screw fixation or OR & IF by k - wires, compression screw or Herbe screw. - Undisplaced ununited (nonunion) fractures may be treated by excavation of the scaphoid & placement of volar inlay coicocancellous bone graft (Matti Russe procedure). In most cases of stable nonunion cancellous bone graft from either the distal radius (for small defects) or the iliac crest (preferable because of its superior osteogenic and mechanical propeies) is packed into the defect. Dorsal cailage is not disturbed. This provides a hinge and facilitates assessment of scaphoid length. If fracture site is angulated or collapsed coico cancellous volar graft is employed to correct the deformity. If the proximal pole is avascular and no significant radiocarpal ahritis is present, revascularization of the scaphoid with a vascularized bone graft from dorsal radius or preferably pronator quadratus graftQ should be performed. Paial radial stylodectomy should be performed in all patients with radiological signs of stage I radioscaphoid ahritis limited to scaphoid and radial styloid. - Once degenerative ahritis is evident at the radio -carpal joint, salvage procedures includes proximal row carpectomy, scaphoid excision and mid carpal ahodesis or total wrist ahrodesis. Clinical Presentation - The patient is usually and adolescent boy or young adult who gives a h/o falling on outstretched hand usually during active spos. Commonly the injury is misinterpreted as "just a sprain". Like colle's it is a supination - dorsiflexion injury. - Fullness & tenderness in anatomical snuff boxQ. Radial side wrist pain; passive dorsiflexion to the radial side is painful, grip is weak and release of grip gives transitory pain, resisted pinch between the thumb and index finger is uncomfoable. Proximal pressure along the axis of the thumb may be painfulQ.

The Dennis stability concept is based on three columns: Anterior, Middle, and Posterior. One of the earliest mechanistic classification schemes for thoracolumbar fractures was given by Dennis, who attempted to elucidate the concept of spinal stability by assigning osseous and soft tissue structures into one of these three columns.

The Anterior column includes the anterior half of the vertebral body and the anterior longitudinal ligament. The Posterior column consists of the posterior half of the vertebral body and disc, as well as the posterior longitudinal ligament. The Posterior elements, including pedicles and facet joints, and the remaining ligaments, also fall within this category.

This system divides thoracolumbar injuries into four principal categories: Compression, Burst, Chance, and Fracture-dislocation. With this paradigm, the greatest emphasis is placed on the Middle column, such that any injuries extending into this portion of the spine are generally assumed to be unstable.

Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells that typically compose about 1% of the red cells. They develop and mature in the bone marrow and then circulate for about a day in the blood before developing into mature red blood cells. Like red blood cells, reticulocytes do not have a nucleus.

Reticulocytes are so named because of a reticular (mesh-like) network of ribosomal RNA that becomes visible under a microscope with supravital stains. They appear slightly bluer than other red cells when viewed with the normal Romanowsky stain.

In certain conditions, such as hemolytic anemia, the body may produce an increased number of reticulocytes to overcome chronic or severe loss of mature red blood cells. This is known as reticulocytosis.

Reticulocyte numbers can also be decreased in various conditions, including chemotherapy, aplastic anemia, iron deficiency anemia, vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency, pernicious anemia, bone marrow malignancies, and anemia of chronic disease.

The essential feature of an autoimmune disease is that tissue injury is caused by the immunologic reaction of the organism with its own tissues. Autoimmunity refers to the presence of antibodies or T lymphocytes that react with self-antigens, but this does not necessarily imply that the development of self-reactivity has pathogenic consequences. Autoimmune diseases are syndromes caused by the activation of T or B cells or both, with no evidence of other causes such as infections or malignancies.

Intense stimulation of T lymphocytes can produce nonspecific signals that bypass the need for antigen-specific helper T cells and lead to polyclonal B-cell activation with the formation of multiple autoantibodies. It is now known that low levels of autoreactivity of T and B cells with self-antigens in the periphery are critical to their survival. Co-stimulatory molecules, such as B7-1 (CD80) or B7-2 (CD86), are involved in autoimmunity.

Gastritis is the inflammation of the gastric mucosa, a histological diagnosis that can be divided into two categories: acute and chronic.

Acute gastritis is a transient mucosal injury, typically associated with neutrophilic infiltration. Important causes of acute gastritis include the heavy use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin, ischemia and shock, severe stress (trauma, burn, surgery), uremia, and nosogastric intubation.

Chronic gastritis, on the other hand, is characterized by the presence of chronic mucosal inflammatory changes, leading to mucosal atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, usually in the absence of erosions. Significant causes of chronic gastritis include Helicobacter pylori infection, autoimmune conditions in association with pernicious anemia, alcohol and smoking, granulomatous conditions such as Crohn's disease, radiation, and miscellaneous conditions like amyloidosis, graft-versus-host disease, and uremia.

Viruses, as obligate intracellular parasites, cannot be grown on inanimate culture medium. Three methods are employed for cultivating viruses: animal inoculation, embryonated eggs, and tissue culture.

Animal inoculation is a common method, where mice are the most widely used animals. Adult mice are typically used, except for coxsackie virus, which is cultivated using suckling mice, as adult mice are not susceptible.

Embryonated eggs are also used for virus cultivation, with different sites of inoculation depending on the virus. The chorioallantoic membrane, amniotic sac, allantoic cavity, and yolk sac are all used for different viruses.

Tissue culture is the most important method for virus isolation and is available in three types: organ culture, explant culture, and cell culture. Cell culture is the most commonly employed method and is further divided into primary cell culture, diploid cell strains, and continuous cell lines.

Primary cell culture cannot be maintained in serial cultures and is typically used for a limited number of passages. Diploid cell strains can be maintained for a limited number of passages, while continuous cell lines can be maintained indefinitely. Examples of continuous cell lines used for virus cultivation include Hela, HEP-2, McCoy, vero cells, BHK, and Detroid-6.

High-density lipoproteins (HDL) play a crucial role in the transport of cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver. The primary apoproteins in HDL are Apo-A1, with smaller amounts of Apo-A2, Apo-C, and Apo-E. HDL serves as a plasma reservoir for Apo-C and Apo-E, which can be transferred to very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) and chylomicrons.

The level of HDL in the serum has significant clinical implications. It is inversely related to the incidence of myocardial infarction, making it an important factor in the development of coronary artery diseases. HDL is often referred to as "good cholesterol" due to its antiatherogenic properties. The "H" in HDL stands for "Healthy", and a level below 35 mg/dl increases the risk of coronary artery diseases, while a level above 60 mg/dl provides protection.

Hypophosphatemia is a complication of refeeding syndrome, which occurs in malnourished patients who are administered with intravenous glucose. During periods of starvation, electrolytes are shifted to the extracellular space to maintain adequate serum concentrations. With refeeding, insulin levels rise and electrolytes are shifted back intracellularly, resulting in potential hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatemia. Additionally, refeeding results in an increased cellular need for phosphorus for energy production (ATP) and glucose metabolism.

Carcinoid tumors arise from the neuroendocrine cells. The majority of these tumors are found in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, with more than 40% occurring in the small intestine, specifically in the jejunum and ileum. The tracheobronchial tree and lungs are the next common sites involved.

The features of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors vary depending on the location. For example, those found in the esophagus, stomach, and proximal small intestine tend to be rare, with less than 1% occurring in these areas. In contrast, carcinoids in the jejunum and ileum are more common, with over 40% occurring in these regions. The duodenum and colorectum are also affected, with carcinoids found in approximately 25% of cases.

The size of carcinoid tumors can vary, with some being small and multiple, while others can be larger and solitary. The secretory products of these tumors also depend on the location, with histamine, somatostatin, and serotonin being produced in some cases, and gastrin, cholecystokinin, and polypeptide YY being produced in others.

Symptoms of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors can include dysphagia, weight loss, and reflux in the esophagus, gastritis and ulcers in the stomach, and abdominal pain and obstruction in the small intestine. In some cases, carcinoids may be asymptomatic and only discovered incidentally, while others may cause symptoms such as biliary obstruction and metastatic disease.

question: In hypovolemic shock % of fluid depletion should be
exp: (B) 15-45% # Treatment should be aggressive and directed more by response to therapy than by initial classification.> Class I hemorrhage (loss of 0-15%):* In the absence of complications, only minimal tachycardia is seen.* Usually, no changes in BP, pulse pressure, or respiratory rate occur.* A delay in capillary refill of longer than 3 seconds corresponds to a volume loss of approximately 10%.> Class II hemorrhage (loss of 15-30%):* Clinical symptoms include tachycardia (rate >100 beats per minute), tachypnea, decrease in pulse pressure, cool clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, and slight anxiety.* The decrease in pulse pressure is a result of increased catecholamine levels, which causes an increase in peripheral vascular resistance and a subsequent increase in the diastolic BP.> Class III hemorrhage (loss of 30-40%):* By this point, patients usually have marked tachypnea and tachycardia, decreased systolic BP, oliguria, and significant changes in mental status, such as confusion or agitation.* In patients without other injuries or fluid losses, 30-40% is the smallest amount of blood loss that consistently causes a decrease in systolic BP.* Most of these patients require blood transfusions, but the decision to administer blood should be based on the initial response to fluids.> Class IV hemorrhage (loss of >40%):* Symptoms include the following: Marked tachycardia, decreased systolic BP, narrowed pulse pressure (or immeasurable diastolic pressure), markedly decreased (or no) urinary output, depressed mental status (or loss of consciousness), and cold and pale skin.

* Type I (most common, occurring in 45% of cases): Anomalous connection at the supracardiac level, where pulmonary veins drain into the left innominate vein or superior vena cava.
* Type II (25%): Anomalous connection at the cardiac level, where pulmonary veins join the coronary sinus or enter the right atrium directly.
* Type III (25%): Anomalous connection at the infracardiac level, where pulmonary veins drain into the portal vein.
* Type IV (5%): Anomalous connection at multiple levels.

Infracardiac type of TAPVC is always obstructive, whereas cardiac and supracardiac types may be obstructive or non-obstructive.

Radiological findings of TAPVC include:

* Cardiomegaly
* Plethoric lung fields
* Snowman or figure of '8' configuration in supracardiac TAPVC
* Ground glass appearance of lung in obstructive TAPVC

Clinical manifestations of TAPVC vary depending on the type:

* Non-obstructive TAPVC: Patients present with mild cyanosis and congestive heart failure at 6-8 weeks.
* Obstructive TAPVC: Patients present with severe cyanosis and congestive heart failure within the first week.

In supracardiac TAPVC, the pulmonary veins join to form a single trunk (common pulmonary vein), which then drains through the anomalous connection.

The common carotid arteries bifurcate at the level of the thyroid cartilage into the external and internal carotid arteries. The external carotid artery sends branches to the neck and face, whereas the internal carotid artery ascends to the base of the skull, entering the carotid canal. Upon exiting the carotid canal, the internal carotid artery courses horizontally over the foramen lacerum and enters the cavernous sinus. After turning superiorly, it divides into its terminal branches.

The terminal branches of the internal carotid artery include the ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating artery, anterior cerebral artery, anterior communicating artery, and middle cerebral artery. The ophthalmic artery courses through the optic canal to supply the retina, orbit, and part of the scalp. The posterior communicating artery joins the posterior cerebral artery with the internal carotid artery. The anterior cerebral artery courses superiorly and then posteriorly along the corpus callosum, providing blood supply to the medial sides of both cerebral hemispheres. The anterior communicating artery is a short artery that connects the two anterior cerebral arteries. The middle cerebral artery courses into the lateral fissure between the parietal and temporal lobes, sending many branches to the lateral sides of the cerebral hemispheres and central branches into the brain.

Type VII Collagen is the major component of anchoring fibrils of the dermoepidermal junction. The dermoepidermal junction, also known as the basement membrane zone (BMZ), can be recognized histologically by staining with PAS stain. Ultrastructural examination of the dermoepidermal junction by electron microscopy shows two distinct layers with different optical densities: the upper, less electron-dense layer, known as the Lamina Lucida, and the lower, more electron-dense layer, known as the Lamina Densa.

The dermoepidermal junction is composed of three components: hemidesmosomes, anchoring filaments, and anchoring fibrils. Hemidesmosomes are multiprotein complexes that facilitate the stable adhesion of basal epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane. The intermediate keratin filaments K5/K14 present within the basal keratinocytes attach to the hemidesmosomes at the base of the cell. The major hemidesmosomal protein is Bullous Pemphigoid Antigen-1 (BPAg1 or BP230), which attaches to the transmembrane component protein BPAg2 (BP 180) below. The other hemidesmosomal protein, Plectin, is attached to the transmembrane component protein called a6b4 integrin below.

Anchoring filaments form the Lamina Lucida layer and consist of Laminin 5/332 proteins that connect BPAg2 and a6b4 integrin above to Lamina Densa below. Lamina Densa is an electron-dense layer present in the dermoepidermal junction, composed mainly of Type IV Collagen. It also contains various other proteins, including Laminin 1/111, BM-40, SPARC, Nidogen, and Perlecan.

Anchoring fibrils are ultrastructurally U-shaped structures that attach the Lamina Densa above to the underlying connective tissue below in the dermis. Type VII Collagen is the major protein in anchoring fibrils.

The hope was that a clearly defined neurochemical abnormality would be identified, providing the basis for the development of rational therapeutic interventions analogous to those used to treat Parkinson's disease.

Schizophrenia is a complex condition characterized by dysregulated levels of serotonin, dopamine, and noradrenaline. While these neurotransmitters are implicated in the disease, a single predominant role has not been established.

Parkinson's disease is caused by the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), resulting in reduced striatal dopamine levels and the formation of intracytoplasmic proteinaceous inclusions known as Lewy bodies.

Alzheimer's disease is associated with a decrease in the cortical levels of several proteins and neurotransmitters, including acetylcholine, its synthetic enzyme choline acetyltransferase, and nicotinic cholinergic receptors.

Hypokalemia has significant effects on cardiac, skeletal, and intestinal muscle cells. One of the prominent effects is the increased risk of ventricular and atrial arrhythmias. Hypokalemia can also predispose to digoxin toxicity by reducing competition between potassium and digoxin for shared binding sites on cardiac Na+/K+-ATPase subunits. Electrocardiographic changes in hypokalemia include broad flat T waves, ST depression, and QT prolongation, which are most pronounced when serum potassium levels are less than 2.7 mmol/L.

Hypokalemia can also lead to skeletal muscle weakness and paralysis due to hyperpolarization, impairing the capacity to depolarize and contract. Additionally, it can cause skeletal myopathy and predispose to rhabdomyolysis. The paralytic effects of hypokalemia on intestinal smooth muscle can cause intestinal ileus.

Hypokalemia can also have functional effects on the kidney, including sodium-chloride and bicarbonate retention, polyuria, phosphaturia, hypocitraturia, and activation of renal ammoniagenesis. Bicarbonate retention and other acid-base effects of hypokalemia can contribute to the generation of metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemic polyuria is caused by a combination of central polydipsia and an AVP-resistant renal concentrating defect.

Structural changes in the kidney due to hypokalemia include a relatively specific vacuolizing injury to proximal tubular cells, interstitial nephritis, and renal cysts. Hypokalemia can also predispose to acute kidney injury and can lead to end-stage renal disease in patients with longstanding hypokalemia, particularly those with eating disorders and/or laxative abuse.

Hypokalemia is also implicated in the pathophysiology and progression of hypertension, heart failure, and stroke. For example, short-term potassium restriction in healthy individuals and patients with essential hypertension induces sodium-chloride retention and hypertension. Correction of hypokalemia is particularly important in hypertensive patients treated with diuretics, in whom blood pressure improves with the establishment of normokalemia.

Hirschsprung's disease, also known as congenital aganglonic megacolon, is caused by the defective migration of neural crest cells into the mesodermal layer of the gut. This results in the absence of ganglions, a type of nerve cell, in a portion of the intestinal tract. The affected segment lacks both the Meissner submucosal and Auerbach myenteric plexuses, which are essential for normal gut function.

question: Alkalinization of urine is done in which of the following drug poisoning? ()
exp: Most drugs taken in overdose are extensively detoxified by the liver to produce inactive metabolites which are voided in the urine. Sometimes hepatic degradation produces active metabolites, but the secondary compounds are then conveed to non-toxic derivatives. Under these circumstances, forced diuresis is inappropriate. The procedure should be undeaken only if the following conditions are satisfied: # A substantial propoion of the drug is excreted unchanged. # The drug is distributed mainly in the extracellular fluid. # The drug is minimally protein-bound. # Principle-- Most drugs are weak electrolytes and exist paly as undissociated molecules at physiological pH. The extent of ionisation is a function of the ionisation constant of the drug (Ka for both acids and bases), and the pH of the medium in which it is dissolved. Ionisation constants are usually expressed in the form of their negative logarithm, pKa. Hence the pKa scale is analogous to the pH notation : the stronger an acid the lower its pKa, and the stronger a base the higher its pKa. Thus when pKa = pH, the concentrations of ionised and non-ionised drugs are equal. Cell membranes are most permeable to substances that are lipid soluble and in the non-ionised, rather than the ionised form. Thus the rate of diffusion from the renal tubular lumen back into the circulation is decreased when a drug is maximally ionised. Because ionisation of acidic drugs is increased in an alkaline environment, and that of basic drugs is increased in an acid solution, manipulation of the urinary pH enhances renal excretion. # Forced alkaline diuresis : This is most useful in the case of phenobarbitone, lithium, and salicylates. Administer 1500 ml of fluid IV, in the first hour as follows : - 500 ml of 5% dextrose - 500 ml of 1.2 or 1.4% sodium bicarbonate - 500 ml of 5% dextrose. # Forced acid diuresis : Forced acid diuresis is no longer recommended for any drug or poison, including amphetamines, strychnine, quinine or phencyclidine. REF:THE SYNOPSIS OF FORENSIC MEDICINE AND TOXICOLOGY:K S NARAYANA REDDY;PAGE NO 289
exp_upd: A variety of poisons, such as iodoacetate, heavy metal ions (lead, mercury), and oxidizing agents act as irreversible non-competitive inhibitors. These inhibitors do not compete with the substrate for binding to the enzyme. Instead, they typically bind to a different domain on the enzyme, distinct from the substrate binding site. Since these inhibitors have no structural resemblance to the substrate, an increase in substrate concentration generally does not relieve this inhibition. The inhibitor forms a covalent bond with the enzyme, rendering the reaction irreversible. As a result, the velocity (Vmax) is reduced. Notably, the remaining enzyme molecules retain their affinity for the substrate, as reflected in the unchanged Km value.

These inhibitors do not compete with the substrate for binding to the enzyme. Instead, they typically bind to a different domain on the enzyme, distinct from the substrate binding site. Since these inhibitors have no structural resemblance to the substrate, an increase in substrate concentration generally does not relieve this inhibition. The inhibitor forms a covalent bond with the enzyme, rendering the reaction irreversible. As a result, the velocity (Vmax) is reduced. Notably, the remaining enzyme molecules retain their affinity for the substrate, as reflected in the unchanged Km value.

question: Mutation leading to sickle cell anemia?
exp: Ans. is D i.e., Point mutation. Sickle cell anemia is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy, i.e., the type of disease characterized by production of defective hemoglobin. Sickle cell anemia results from mutation in b-globin gene. It is caused by a point mutation (Base substitution mutation) at the sixth position of the b-globin chain leading to subsitution of a valine residue for a glutamic acid residue resulting in sickle hemoglobin (HbS). Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder. If an individual is homozygous for the sickle cell mutation, almost all the hemoglobin in the red cell is HbS. In heterozyogotes, only about 40% of the hemoglobin is HbS, the remainder being normal hemoglobins.

Tuberculous meningitis is a serious and potentially life-threatening condition characterized by a gradual onset of fever over a period of two weeks, accompanied by symptoms such as vomiting, altered sensorium, and characteristic basal exudates and hydrocephalus on cranial CT scans. The condition typically arises from the formation of metastatic caseous lesions in the cerebral cortex or meningitis that develops during the lymphohaematogenous spread of primary infection.

The initial lesion grows and discharges tubercle bacilli into the subarachnoid space, resulting in the formation of a gelatinous basal exudate that obstructs the normal flow of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in and out of the ventricular system at the level of the basal cisterns, leading to communicating hydrocephalus.

The clinical course of tuberculous meningitis can be divided into three stages. The prodromal stage, or stage of invasion, is marked by an insidious onset of symptoms, including headache, vomiting, low-grade fever, loss of appetite, photophobia, and disturbed sleep. The stage of meningitis is characterized by signs of meningeal irritation, such as neck rigidity and Kernig's sign. The stage of coma is marked by loss of consciousness, bradycardia, dilated and fixed pupils, and Cheyne-Stokes or Biot-type respiration, as well as episodic decerebration.

CT scans of patients with tuberculous meningitis typically show obliteration of the basal cisterns by isodense or hyperdense exudate, with avid enhancement of the basal meninges extending into the ambient, Sylvian, pontine, and chiasmatic cisterns. Hydrocephalus is present in 45-87% of patients at the time of diagnosis.

Behavioral therapy, developed by BF Skinner, posits that all behaviors are learned phenomena and can be unlearned. There are three primary types of reinforcement in this context. Positive reinforcement occurs when a behavior is rewarded, increasing the likelihood of its repetition. For instance, if a behavior is rewarded with a desirable outcome, it is more likely to be repeated.

Negative reinforcement, on the other hand, involves the removal of an aversive response following a behavior, leading to its repetition. For example, a person may delete all messages before meeting their girlfriend to avoid an argument, which would be an aversive response. This behavior is repeated because the aversive response is removed.

Extinction is a type of reinforcement where a behavior is performed, but the rewarding response is removed, decreasing the likelihood of its repetition. In this scenario, a child may enjoy playing with others, but when they engage in undesirable behavior, such as fighting, they are removed from the activity. This reduction in reward leads to a decrease in the undesirable behavior.

Amino acids are classified into four groups based on their polarity, which reflects their functional role in protein structure. The polarity of an amino acid determines its ability to participate in protein interactions and shape the three-dimensional structure of a protein.

Non-polar amino acids, also known as hydrophobic amino acids, have no charge on their 'R' group. This group includes eight amino acids: alanine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and proline.

Polar amino acids with no charge on their 'R' group carry no charge, but possess functional groups such as hydroxyl, sulfhydryl, and amide, which participate in hydrogen bonding with other amino acids. This group includes seven amino acids: glycine, serine, threonine, cysteine, glutamine, asparagine, and tyrosine.

Polar amino acids with a positive 'R' group include three amino acids: lysine, arginine, and histidine.

Polar amino acids with a negative 'R' group are the dicarboxylic monoamino acids aspartic acid and glutamic acid.

Membrane proteins are integral (transmembrane) proteins, including ion pumps (such as Na+-K+ ATPase) and channels, which are globular and amphipathic, consisting of two hydrophilic ends separated by an intervening hydrophobic region that traverses the hydrophobic core of the bilayer. These proteins interact with the fatty acyl groups of phospholipids in the cell membrane and require the use of detergents for their solubilization. Integral proteins are asymmetrically distributed across the membrane bilayer.

Peripheral proteins, on the other hand, are present on the surface of the membrane and do not penetrate all the way through. They are located on both surfaces of the membrane, outer and inner. Peripheral proteins do not interact directly with the phospholipid bilayer. Instead, they bind to the hydrophilic regions of transmembrane proteins through electrostatic and hydrogen bonds. Some peripheral proteins bind to the membrane via a covalently attached lipid anchor, interacting with polar lipid head groups in the membrane. As they do not interact directly with the hydrophobic core of phospholipids, they do not require the use of detergents for their release. They can be released by treatment with salt solutions of high ionic strength.

Peripheral proteins serve as cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) that anchor cells to neighboring cells and to basal lamina. They also contribute to the cytoskeleton when present on the inside of the membrane, such as spectrin, ankyrin, and band 4.1 in red blood cells.

The important functions of cell membrane proteins include:

* Channels (pores)
* Receptors
* Enzymes
* Carrier proteins
* Ion pumps
* Adhesion molecules
* Enzymes
* Controllers of the transport of substances

Succinylcholine (Suxamethonium) is a depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant that causes sustained partial depolarization of muscle end plates. Initially, it produces twitching and fasciculation, followed by flaccid paralysis. It is the shortest and fastest acting skeletal muscle relaxant, and it is the only muscle relaxant that stimulates autonomic ganglia and the vagus, leading to bradycardia.

Succinylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase, and some patients have genetically determined abnormalities or deficiencies of pseudocholinesterase, which can lead to a phase II block (dual block). This muscle relaxant can cause muscle fasciculations and soreness, changes in blood pressure and heart rate, arrhythmia, histamine release, and potassium efflux from muscles.

Post-operative muscle pain (myalgia, muscle soreness) is a common problem associated with succinylcholine use. Additionally, succinylcholine can accentuate malignant hyperthermia caused by halothane, and it is the most common cause of malignant hyperthermia. Succinylcholine can also cause dangerous hyperkalemia in patients with certain conditions, such as burns, massive trauma, crush injury, severe intra-abdominal infection, spinal cord injury, hemiplegia/paraplegia, muscular dystrophy, Guillian-Barré syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, severe Parkinsonism, tetanus, polyneuropathy, closed head injury, stroke, encephalitis, and myasthenia gravis.

Succinylcholine increases all pressures, including intraocular, intracranial, blood pressure, and intrabdominal pressure. It can also cause trismus (masseter spasm), especially in patients susceptible to malignant hyperthermia.

Adenocarcinoma of the kidney, also known as hypernephroma or Grawitz's tumor, is the most common neoplasm (75%) of the kidney. It arises from renal tubular cells, most commonly occurring on the upper pole. The tumor is prone to grow into the renal vein, and highly vascular metastases may pulsate. If the tumor extends beyond the renal capsule, it is liable to metastasize via the lymph nodes in the hilum of the kidney to the para-aortic nodes and beyond.

The most common symptom of hypernephroma is hematuria, which is often accompanied by other paraneoplastic symptoms such as PUO, polycythaemia, hypercalcaemia, anaemia, and others. Metastases occur via the bloodstream to bone, liver, and lung, with renal vein extension potentially embolizing to the pulmonary circulation during nephrectomy.

In men, a rapidly developing varicocele is a rare but impressive sign, often occurring on the left side due to obstruction of the left gonadal vein where it joins the left renal vein. Atypical presentations may include hyperpyrexia, extreme anemia, or polycythemia (occurring in 4% of cases), hypercalcemia, and nephrotic syndrome.

Investigation typically begins with ultrasound, which is often the initial or screening tool of choice. Computed tomography (CT) with contrast demonstrates the extent of the lesion more clearly and shows whether there is hilar lymphadenopathy or renal vein involvement. Magnetic resonance venography (MRV) remains the best choice for detecting renal vein invasion.

Treatment for hypernephroma typically involves nephrectomy with removal of the perinephric fat, which can be performed through a loin or transverse or oblique upper abdominal incision. The transabdominal approach allows for wider exposure of the renal pedicle and inferior vena cava. The vascular pedicle should be ligated before the kidney is mobilized to prevent the release of malignant cells into the circulation. Adenocarcinoma of the kidney does not respond well to radiotherapy or conventional chemotherapy, although early promising results have been reported from clinical trials of the cytokine interleukin-2. Conventional surgical treatment may involve nephroureterectomy, while percutaneous resection is controversial.

Wilms' tumor, also known as nephroblastoma, is a mixed tumor containing epithelial and connective tissue elements arising from embryonic nephrogenic tissue. The tumors are usually discovered during the first four years of life and are characterized by an abdominal tumor that grows rapidly while the child's general well-being deteriorates. Pyrexia, which is a feature in half of these patients, often disappears when the tumor is removed. Metastasis occurs early, mainly to the lungs, with liver and bone metastases being rare and brain metastases even more so. Lymphatic spread is uncommon, and the presence of bone secondaries favors a diagnosis of nephroblastoma, another renal tumor of childhood. Treatment typically involves nephrectomy followed by radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy, and partial nephrectomy may be possible in patients with bilateral disease. The prognosis is generally good for children under one year of age, with 80% surviving for five years, but the prognosis is less good in older children. Recurrences often occur within a year, and a child surviving for 18 months or more is likely cured.

Entropy monitoring is a method of assessing the effect of certain anaesthetic drugs on the brain's electroencephalogram (EEG). This technique was commercially developed by Datex-Ohmeda, now part of GE Healthcare. Entropy is a quantitative EEG device that captures a single-lead frontal EEG signal using a 3-electrode sensor applied to the patient's forehead. The system assesses the degree of irregularity in EEG signals, with the principle being that the irregularity of an EEG signal decreases with increasing brain levels of anaesthetic drugs. Entropy is a measure of this irregularity.

The Entropy monitor generates two numbers derived from different frequency bands. The State Entropy (SE) is calculated from the 0.8Hz to 32Hz range, while the Response Entropy (RE) uses frequencies up to 47Hz. Electromyogram activity is more prominent in higher frequencies, which may cause the Response Entropy to respond more quickly when muscle activity is present. Published studies have shown that Entropy values relate to clinical levels of anaesthetic depth. Most commonly used anaesthetic drugs are detectable by Entropy monitoring, with the notable exception of nitrous oxide, similar to BIS monitoring.

A Hill-Sachs lesion typically occurs as a result of recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation, where the humeral head compresses against the anteroinferior part of the glenoid, causing a posterolateral compression fracture of the humeral head. This is often accompanied by a Banka lesion, which involves the stripping of the glenoidal labrum and periosteum from the anterior surface of the glenoid and scapular neck.

The lesion is best visualized on plain films following joint relocation, particularly on internal rotation views. It appears as a sclerotic vertical line running from the top of the humeral head towards the shaft, and if large, may exhibit a wedge-shaped defect.

Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) are highly sensitive to this lesion, which appears as a region of flattening or a wedge-shaped defect, with bone marrow edema on MRI in acute cases, involving the posterolateral humeral head above the level of the coracoid. This is typically seen in the superior few slices, where the humeral head should be rounded. It is essential to note that below the level of the coracoid, the humeral head normally flattens out posterolaterally, and this should not be misinterpreted as a Hill-Sachs lesion.

exp_upd: Myocardial oxygen demand and consumption are directly proportional to heart rate and systemic arterial pressure. Myocardial efficiency is lowest when the heart is contracting against a greater afterload or aerial resistance. It is also less efficient with increasing heart rate. Conversely, myocardial efficiency is most economical when stroke volume is greater, with afterload and heart rate kept constant. Even in a quiescent heart, the myocardium extracts 75-80% of the oxygen delivered to it, which is the highest percentage in the body. Myocardial oxygen usage is most closely related to the total tension developed by the ventricular muscle. Pulmonary venous hypertension is caused by increased resistance to blood flow in the pulmonary veins, resulting from obstruction or reduced compliance within the left atrium, mitral valve, or left ventricle. This condition is classified into three grades of severity.

Grade I pulmonary venous hypertension is characterized by reversal of the normal gravity-dependent gradient of pulmonary blood flow, enlargement of the right superior pulmonary vein, and loss of visibility of the mid and distal portions of the right descending pulmonary trunk.

Grade II pulmonary venous hypertension is marked by interstitial pulmonary edema and pleural effusion.

Grade III pulmonary venous hypertension is accompanied by alveolar pulmonary edema, with bilateral fluffy alveolar opacities and cardiomegaly, left atrial enlargement.

Pathophysiology 1. Cross reactivity of host antistreptococcal antibodies to cardiac antigens 2. Microbe initiated autoimmune reactivity. Jones Criteria for Diagnosis of Rheumatic Fever Major Criteria Carditis Pancarditis, seen in 50-60% of patients, develops within the first 2 weeks of rheumatic fever. Pericarditis is evidenced by presence of a pericardial rub, myocarditis by tachycardia, soft S1, presence of S3 and CCF and endocarditis by the presence of Carey-Coombs' murmur (mitral diastolic murmur). Ahritis (60-75%) Flitting and fleeting type of polyahritis involving large joints with no residual deformity is seen in 60-75% of patients and occurs early in rheumatic fever. Jaccod's ahritis: Ulnar detion of 4th and 5th finger with flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints is the only residual deformity seen in rheumatic polyahritis. Subcutaneous Nodules Non-tender nodules are seen over bony prominences like elbows, shin, occiput, spine in 3-5% of patients and occur 3-6 weeks after onset of rheumatic fever. Patients who have subcutaneous nodules almost always have carditis. Erythema Marginatum (< 5% and evanescent) Macular lesions with an erythematous rim and central clearing in a bathing suit distribution are seen in < 5% of patients and occur early in rheumatic fever. Chorea (Sydenham's Chorea) (2-30%) A neurological disorder with rapid, involuntary and purposeless non-repetitive movements with a self limiting course of 2-6 weeks is more common in females and is a late manifestation of rheumatic fever. Minor Criteria Clinical 1. Fever 2. Ahralgia 3. Previous history of rheumatic fever or rheumatic hea disease. Laboratory 1. Acute phase reactants (leucocytosis, raised ESR, C-reactive protein) 2. Prolonged PR interval in ECG (> 0.2 sec). WHO Criteria Jones major and pa of the minor criteria except prior history of rheumatic fever/rheumatic hea disease and C-reactive protein. Essential Criteria Evidence for recent streptococcal infection as evidenced by1. Increase in ASO titre a. > 333 Todd units (in children) b. > 250 Todd units (in adults). 2. Positive throat culture for streptococcal infection. 3. Recent history of scarlet fever. Two major (or) one major and two minor criteria, in the presence of essential criteria, is required to diagnose Acute Rheumatic Fever. question: A patient is found to be positive for HBs Ag on routine laboratory evaluation. Other serological tests for hepatitis are unremarkable. He is clinically asymptomatic and liver enzymes are within the normal range. Which of the following best describes his diagnosis:
exp: Answer is A (Inactive HBV carrier) Absence of clinical signs and symptoms of liver damage and normal liver enzymes in an HBs Ag positive individual with otherwise unremarkable serological tests suggests a diagnosis of Inactive HBV carrier state. 'An inactive hepatitis B carrier is defined as one with HBs Ag in serum hut without HBe Ag with normal liver function tests and with low/ undetectable levels of HBV DNA (< 103-104 virions/ml) - 'Blue Prints Pocket Gastroenterology' by Grover (Lippincott Williams) 1st (2007) /114 Chronic Hepatitis B carriers (HBs Ag + ye with IgG Anti HBc) Chronic Hepatitis B virus carriers can be divided into two categories based on activity of the virus and evidence of liver damage Inactive HBs Ag Carrier state Patients with negligible virus replication (HBV DNA levels < 103 virions/m1) and /or no clinical signs and symptoms of liver damage and normal liver enzyme levels are characterized as inactive HBV carriers Inactive HBV carriers harbor Hepatitis B virus antigen (HBs Ag), but are clinically asymptomatic, have a normal physical examination with normal liver enzymes (AST & ALT). HBe Ag is typically negative and levels of HBV DNA are less than 103-104 virions/ml Such patients have minimal (if any) liver inflammation or damage, and usually live a normal life. However compared to the general population these patients remain at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma Treatment is currently not recommended for Inactive HBV carrier. However regular observation is advised as there is a risk for reactivation of virus. Chronic Hepatitis B (Active) Patients with active virus replication ( HBV DNA levels > 103 -104 virions/ml) and /or clinical signs and symptoms of liver damage or elevated liver enzyme levels are characterized as chronic hepatitis B patients. Depending on the presence or absence of HBe Ag two type of chronic (active) hepatitis B may be identified. HBe Ag positive chronic hepatitis B These HBs Ag positive, individuals are also positive for HBe Ag and show detectable HBV DNA levels. Such patients are in the replicative phase of chronic hepatitis B infection, have persistently or intermittently elevated liver enzymes and liver biopsy results typically reveals inflammation and damage Patients with chronic (active) hepatitis B may become inactive (relatively non replicative) over time (rate of L-10 % per year) by becoming negative for HBe Ag and HBV DNA (HBV DNA < 10' - 104) virions/ml) Liver injury tend to subside in such patients and these may then be characterized as 'inactive carriers' HBe Ag negative chronic hepatitis B (Precore mutant) Such HBs Ag positive individuals are negative for HBe Ag but show detectable HBV DNA levels. Such patients are also in the replicative phase of chronic hepatitis B (despite negative HBe Ag) and have persistently or intermittently elevated liver enzymes and liver biopsy results typically reveal severe inflammation and damage Negative HBe Ag Status results from a mutant strain of hepatitis B that is characterized by the .failure of the virus to make the hepatitis B 'e' antigen (HBe Ag). This mutation is called the `precore' mutation as it prevents the translation of a precore protein to prevent HBe antigen production. This mutation does not however affect the ability of the virus to replicate

Oogenesis refers to the process of formation of ova from the primitive germ cells. Unlike the fetal testis, which begins spermatogenesis at puberty, the fetal ovary begins oogenesis by 10 weeks of gestation. The sequence of events in oogenesis involves the following steps:

The primitive germ cells undergo mitotic divisions to form oogonia, diploid cells. Oogonium is unique in that it is the only female cell in which both 'X' chromosomes are active. The oogonia proliferate by mitosis to form primary oocytes, also diploid cells.

Primary oocytes, formed from the oogonia, enter a prolonged prophase (diplotene stage) of the first meiotic division and remain in this stage until ovulation occurs after puberty. At puberty, primary oocytes complete the first meiotic division to form a secondary oocyte (haploid cell) and the first polar body.

The secondary oocyte immediately begins the second meiotic division, but this division stops at metaphase and is completed only if the mature ovum (ootid) is fertilized with sperm. At that time, the second polar body (polocyte) is extruded, and the fertilized ovum proceeds to form a new individual. Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube.

Protease inhibitors are a class of antiretroviral medications that target the protease enzyme, which plays a crucial role in the maturation of new HIV particles. These medications bind to the protease molecule, interfering with its cleaving function and preventing the production of infectious viral progeny. As they act at a late stage in the viral replication cycle, protease inhibitors are effective in both newly and chronically infected cells.

Ritonavir, a potent protease inhibitor, also exhibits potent inhibitory effects on the cytochrome P450 3A4 enzyme. Saquinavir, on the other hand, is available in two formulations with differing oral bioavailability. The tablet form has a large load and is associated with frequent side effects, including photosensitivity. Saquinavir is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4.

In addition to its antiretroviral effects, ritonavir has been shown to have a broader spectrum of activity than other antifungal medications, such as ketoconazole and fluconazole. Its metabolism is largely dependent on the liver enzyme CYP3A4, resulting in the production of an active metabolite that is excreted in the feces.

Mature dendritic cells play a crucial role in the activation and proliferation of naive T cells. Naive T cells are newly produced T cells that arise from the immune system's production of fresh cells in the bone marrow. These cells respond to newly encountered pathogens containing antigens that the immune system has not processed before. The activation and proliferation of naive T cells create an acquired immunity to the newly encountered pathogen.

After the disease is eradicated, a small portion of the T cell population, engendered by the activated naive T cells, constitutes a reservoir of memory T cells. These memory T cells can proliferate and respond quickly to the recurrence of disease.

The proliferation of naive T cells is stimulated by dendritic cells and dendritic cell-derived cytokines, which are the most potent stimulators of this process.

question: A 30 yr old male patient presented with massive haemetemesis. Upper GI endoscopy shows a 2x2 cm ulcer on the posterior aspect of the first pa of the duodenum. Bleeding vessel is seen, but could not be controlled endoscopically. Patient's pulse rate is 100, BP 110/70, Hb 10 gms% after blood transfusion. What will be the next line of management is:
exp: Duodenotomy, with ligation of bleeding vessel, truncal vagotomy with pyloroplasty. The surgical treatment for peptic ulcer disease has changed dramatically. The elective operations for peptic ulcer disease have been viually eliminated! Antibiotics have become primary anti-ulcer therapy with the realization that in most cased, peptic ulceration is an infectious disease. Operative interventions are now reserved for complications of the ulcer disease. 3 complications are most common: - hemorrhage - perforation - obstruction For gastric ulcers, surgical indications also include intractability or nonhealing of the ulcer because of the risk of cancer. Management of hemorrhage: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is the intial diagnostic test if peptic ulcer is suspected, following resuscitation. Endoscopy is able to identify the site and source of bleeding in over 90 % of patients. First line of treatment for bleeding ulcer is endoscopic hemostasis. Methods of endoscopic therapy include: -Thermal coagulation by bipolar electrocoagulation or - Direct application of heat through a heater probe or - Injection of epinephrine into the base of the bleeding peptic ulcer Operative intervention is required when -The endoscopic treatment fails - There is massive hemorrhage leading to shock or cardiovascular instability - Prolonged blood loss requiring continuing transfusion - Recurrent hemorrhage requiring hospitalization Emergent operative therapy consists of duodenotomy with direct suture ligagtion of the bleeding vessel in the ulcer base. Post operatively patients are given antibiotic therapy against H. pylori. According to Maingot- role of acid reducing surgeries like vagotomy have decreased significantly. But steps like vagotomy combined with pyloroplasty or antrectomy are still being performed depending on individual preferences to cure the ulcer. Here this patient not controlled by endoscopic methods should undergo emergent surgery consisting of only duodenotomy and bleeding vessel ligation. But since this is not one of the options we would choose the one with the least morbidity. As mentioned above another indication for surgery in gastric ulcer is failure of a recurrent ulcer to respond to medical therapy. This is because of the risk of cancer in nonhealing gastric ulcer (there is no such risk in duodenal ulcer). For benign gastric ulcer, the elective operation of choice is usually a distal gastrectomy including the ulcer with either gastroduodenal (Billroth I) or gastrojejunal (Billroth 11) anastomosis.
opb: Paial gastrectomy including the bleeding segment
opc: Duodenotomy, with ligation of bleeding vessel, truncal vagotomy with pyloroplasty
opd: Duodenotomy, ligation of bleeding vessel with truncal vagotomy, antrectomy

Descriptive epidemiology aims to study the distribution of disease in time, place, and person. Time distribution involves three kinds of trends or fluctuations in disease occurrence: short-term fluctuations, secular trends, and periodic fluctuations.

Short-term fluctuations include epidemics, which are sudden and brief events. There are three major types of epidemics: common-source epidemics, propagated epidemics, and slow (modern) epidemics.

Common-source epidemics occur when the source of the disease agent is the same for all cases. This type of epidemic can be further divided into two categories: single exposure or point source epidemics and continuous or multiple exposure epidemics.

Single exposure or point source epidemics involve a brief and simultaneous exposure to the disease agent, resulting in a rapid rise and fall of cases. The epidemic curve tends to be explosive, with cases clustering within a narrow interval of time. Examples of point source epidemics include food poisoning, the Bhopal gas tragedy, Minamata disease in Japan, and the Chernobyl tragedy.

Continuous or multiple exposure epidemics, on the other hand, involve prolonged and repeated exposure to the disease agent from a common source. This type of epidemic can occur over a longer period, with cases developing at different times. For example, a prostitute may be a common source in a gonorrhea outbreak, but since she will infect her clients over a period of time, the outbreak may not exhibit an explosive rise in cases.

Microscopic angiitisAnti-Glomerular Basement Membrane Antibody (Type I) Crescentic Glomerulonephritis* Anti-GBM antibody crescentic glomerulonephritis, or type I CrGN, is characterized by linear deposits of IgG and, in many cases, C3 on the GBM, as described above. In some of these individuals the anti-GBM antibodies also bind to pulmonary alveolar capillary basement membranes to produce the clinical picture of pulmonary hemorrhages associated with renal failure. These persons are said to have Goodpasture syndrome, to distinguish their condition from socalled idiopathic cases in which renal involvement occurs in the absence of pulmonary disease. Anti-GBM antibodies are present in the serum and are helpful in diagnosis. It is important to recognize type I CrGN because these individuals benefit from plasmapheresis, which removes pathogenic antibodies from the circulation.* Immune Complex-Mediated (Type II) Crescentic Glomerulonephritis* Type II CrGNs are immune complex-mediated disorders. This can be a complication of any of the immune complex nephritides, including poststreptococcal GN, SLE, IgA nephropathy, and Henoch-Schonlein purpura. In some cases, immune complexes can be demonstrated but the underlying cause is undetermined. In all of these cases, immunofluorescence studies reveal the characteristic granular ("lumpy bumpy") pattern of staining of the GBM and/or mesangium for immunoglobulin and/or complement. These individuals cannot usually be helped by plasmapheresis.Pauci-Immune (Type III) Crescentic GlomerulonephritisType III CrGN, also called pauci-immune type CrGN, is defined by the lack of anti-GBM antibodies or significant immune complex deposition detectable by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy. Most of these individuals have antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies in the serum, which, as we have seen, have a role in some vasculitides. Therefore, in some cases type III CrGN is a component of a systemic vasculitis such as microscopic polyangiitis or Wegener granulomatosis. In many cases, however, pauci-immune CrGN is limited to the kidney and is thus called idiopathic

Type I (Von Gierke's disease) and Type VI (Her's disease) are two distinct forms of glycogen storage disease. The key difference between these two types lies in the specific enzyme deficiency.

Type I, also known as Von Gierke's disease, is characterized by a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase, an enzyme that plays a crucial role in both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. This deficiency leads to impaired gluconeogenesis, resulting in severe hypoglycemia and ketosis.

In contrast, Type VI, also known as Her's disease, is caused by a deficiency of glycogen phosphorylase, which is responsible for glycogenolysis. This deficiency does not affect gluconeogenesis, and as a result, patients with Type VI disease typically experience mild hypoglycemia without ketosis.

Motilin is a hormone released by the small intestine during the fasting state. Its blood levels wax and wane, correlating with the initiation and ending of migrating motor complexes (MMC). The MMC typically begins in the stomach and, over a 90-120 minute period, migrates to the ileum, where it dies out. As one complex dies out in the ileum, another begins in the stomach, provided the fasting state continues. Eating a meal interrupts the MMC activity.

Cholecystokinin is released during the intestinal phase of the digestive period, evoked by the presence of fat and protein digestion products in the duodenum. It induces contraction of the gallbladder and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.

Gastrin is released from G cells in the antrum, mostly during the gastric phase of the digestive period. It tends to increase stomach motility, although the rate of emptying is decreased because gastrin also causes the pyloric sphincter to contract. Gastrin may also contribute to the increase in ileal and colonic motility as part of the gastroileal and gastrocolic reflexes, respectively. Gastrin-releasing peptide mediates the neural release of gastrin. Antral enteric neurons, activated by vagal efferents or local reflexes, release gastrin-releasing peptide, which stimulates the G cells to secrete gastrin.
